chapters.n: Second Chronicles opens with Solomon securely established as king. The key to his success is stated first: the Lord was with him and made him great.

f.w: the LORD his God was with him

chapters.n: Solomon begins his reign by calling together the nation’s leaders — military officers, judges, governors, and family heads — to worship with him. He starts with God, not with politics.
They travel to Gibeon, a few miles northwest of Jerusalem, where Moses’ wilderness tabernacle still stood. The Chronicler explains why worship there was legitimate.

f.g: A town about six miles (10 km) northwest of Jerusalem.
A raised worship site; this one was approved because the tabernacle stood there.

chapters.n: At this time Israel’s worship was split in two: the ark was in a tent David had pitched in Jerusalem, while the tabernacle and altar remained at Gibeon. The temple would reunite them.
The bronze altar made by Bezaleel in Moses’ day stood at Gibeon. Solomon and the people came to seek the Lord there, linking his reign to Israel’s ancient worship.

f.g: The Spirit-filled craftsman who built the tabernacle furnishings.
Went there to seek the Lord, to inquire of Him in worship.

chapters.n: Solomon offered a thousand burnt offerings — an extravagant act of devotion, showing his whole heart was turned toward God.
That night God appeared and offered Solomon anything he wished. It is a test of the heart: what would you ask for?

f.w: Ask what I shall give thee

chapters.n: Solomon begins with gratitude, recognizing that God showed great kindness to David and that his own kingship came from that mercy.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed — steadfast, covenant love and loyal kindness.

chapters.n: He asks God to fulfill His promise to David. Solomon feels the weight of ruling a nation as numerous as the dust — echoing God’s promise to Abraham.

f.w: like the dust of the earth

chapters.n: Solomon asks for wisdom and knowledge to lead and judge such a great people. “Go out and come in” means to lead in all of daily life, including war and public affairs.

f.g: Hebrew idiom for leading the people in all activities.

chapters.n: God is pleased that Solomon asked unselfishly — not for wealth, honor, revenge on enemies, or long life, but for wisdom to serve God’s people.

f.w: Because this was in thine heart

chapters.n: God grants wisdom and adds what Solomon didn’t ask for: unmatched riches and honor. When we seek first what God values, He often adds other blessings.
Solomon returns from Gibeon to Jerusalem to begin his reign in earnest.
Solomon builds a large chariot army and stations it in special chariot cities. Notably, Moses’ law had warned kings against multiplying horses.

f.g: Garrison towns built to house chariots and horses.

chapters.n: A picture of overflowing prosperity: silver and gold as common as rocks, and costly cedar as plentiful as the ordinary sycamore-fig trees of the foothills.

f.g: Sycamore-figs, common trees in Judah’s lowland, used for ordinary timber.
The Shephelah, the low hills west of Judah.

chapters.n: Solomon imported horses from Egypt and another source; his traders bought them at set prices. The Hebrew word translated “linen yarn” is now usually read as the place-name Kue (Cilicia).

f.g: Many scholars read Hebrew miqveh/qeve as ‘from Kue’ — Cilicia, in modern Turkey, a horse-trading region.

chapters.n: Solomon’s merchants acted as middlemen, selling chariots and horses to Hittite and Syrian kings. The details show how wealthy and far-reaching his trade had become.

f.g: A shekel weighed about 11.5 grams (0.4 oz).
Here, the neo-Hittite kingdoms of northern Syria.

chapters.n: Solomon resolves to build two houses: a temple for the Lord’s name and a royal palace. The temple comes first in his heart and in the Chronicler’s story.

f.g: God’s ‘name’ stands for His presence, authority, and character dwelling among His people.

chapters.n: Solomon organizes a huge labor force: 70,000 carriers, 80,000 stonecutters in the hills, and 3,600 supervisors.

f.g: Counted out or assigned.
Seventy thousand (a score = 20).

chapters.n: Solomon writes to Huram (also called Hiram), king of the Phoenician port of Tyre, asking for the same help he had given David in building his palace.

f.g: Spelled Hiram in Kings; Tyre was a wealthy Phoenician sea-trading city on the coast of modern Lebanon.

chapters.n: Solomon explains the temple’s purpose: a place dedicated to God for incense, the bread of the Presence, and daily, weekly, monthly, and festival sacrifices — a lasting pattern of worship.

f.g: Symbol of prayer rising to God.
The first day of each month, marked by special offerings.

chapters.n: The temple must be great because Israel’s God is greater than all the so-called gods of the nations.

f.w: great is our God above all gods

chapters.n: Solomon humbly admits that no building could contain God, whom even the highest heavens cannot hold. The temple is a place to meet and worship Him, not to box Him in.

f.w: heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain him

chapters.n: Solomon asks for a master craftsman skilled in metals, dyed fabrics, and engraving to work alongside the artisans David had already gathered.

f.g: Skillful (the KJV meaning, without any sense of trickery).
To engrave or carve.
Expensive dyed threads, like those used in the tabernacle; Tyre was famous for purple dye.

chapters.n: He also requests cedar, cypress, and algum wood from Lebanon, acknowledging that Tyre’s woodsmen are the experts. His own workers will work beside them.

f.g: A prized, uncertain wood (perhaps red sandalwood or juniper), called almug in Kings.
Probably cypress or juniper.

chapters.n: Solomon needs a great amount of timber because the temple is to be “wonderful great” — astonishingly magnificent.

f.g: Extraordinarily great; marvelous.

chapters.n: In payment Solomon offers large amounts of wheat, barley, wine, and olive oil for Huram’s workers — Israel’s farm produce in exchange for Phoenicia’s timber.

f.g: Hebrew kor, a dry measure of roughly 6 bushels (about 220 liters).
A liquid measure of about 6 gallons (22 liters).

chapters.n: Huram replies in writing with a gracious compliment: Solomon’s kingship is evidence of the Lord’s love for His people.

f.w: Because the LORD hath loved his people

chapters.n: Remarkably, this foreign king blesses Israel’s God as the Creator of heaven and earth and praises Him for giving David a wise son.

f.g: Endowed with good sense and insight.

chapters.n: Huram sends a skilled, gifted craftsman — also named Huram (Huram-abi). “Of Huram my father’s” is probably a title like “my master craftsman.”

f.g: Hebrew Huram-abi; ‘abi’ (my father) may be an honorific meaning master or counselor.

chapters.n: This craftsman had an Israelite mother from Dan and a Tyrian father. He was skilled in nearly every material and could design whatever was asked of him — like Bezaleel and Aholiab of old.

f.g: 1 Kings 7:14 says his mother was from Naphtali; perhaps her family had ties to both tribes.
Work out any design given to him.

chapters.n: Huram agrees to the payment Solomon offered and asks that it be sent.

f.g: A polite, deferential way of addressing Solomon.

chapters.n: Tyre’s workers would cut the logs, bind them into rafts, and float them down the coast to Joppa, Israel’s port, from which Solomon’s men would haul them up to Jerusalem.

f.g: Rafts of logs tied together.
Modern Jaffa, near Tel Aviv — the same port Jonah sailed from.

chapters.n: Solomon takes a census of foreigners living in Israel — descendants of the earlier Canaanite peoples — following David’s earlier count. They number 153,600.

f.g: Non-Israelite residents of the land.

chapters.n: These resident foreigners are assigned as carriers, stonecutters, and overseers. The verse repeats the figures from verse 2, framing the chapter.

f.w: to set the people a work
f.g: To keep the people working; to supervise them.

chapters.n: This is the only place the Bible names the temple site “mount Moriah.” It ties together Abraham’s near-sacrifice of Isaac and the spot where God stopped the plague in David’s day — a place of substitution and mercy that points to Christ.

f.w: the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite
f.g: Ornan is called Araunah in Samuel.

chapters.n: Construction began in the second month of Solomon’s fourth year, about 966 BC — a date remembered as a turning point in Israel’s history.

f.w: the fourth year of his reign

chapters.n: The main building was 60 cubits long and 20 wide (about 90 by 30 feet). The “first measure” refers to the older, longer cubit.

f.g: The older royal cubit, about 20.6 inches (52 cm), slightly longer than the common cubit.
A cubit was the length from elbow to fingertip, roughly 18 inches (45 cm).

chapters.n: The front porch was 20 cubits wide. Its listed height of 120 cubits is surprisingly tall; some ancient manuscripts read 20, which fits better. Its interior was gold-covered.

f.g: Some Greek and Syriac texts read ‘twenty cubits’; the figure may reflect a copying difference.

chapters.n: The main hall (the holy place) was paneled with cypress, covered with fine gold, and decorated with palm trees and chain designs — images recalling the garden of Eden and the tree of life.

f.g: Paneled or lined.
Symbols of life, victory, and paradise.

chapters.n: Precious stones adorned the house, and the gold came from Parvaim, a place famous for fine gold but whose location is now unknown.

f.g: An unidentified gold-producing region, perhaps in Arabia.

chapters.n: Beams, door frames, walls, and doors were all covered in gold, and cherubim were engraved on the walls — heavenly guardians of God’s presence, like those guarding Eden.

f.g: Angelic beings who guard sacred space. (The Hebrew plural is already ‘cherubim’; KJV adds an extra -s.)

chapters.n: The most holy place was a perfect cube, 20 cubits each way, covered with 600 talents of fine gold. It was the most sacred room on earth to Israel, where God’s presence dwelt.

f.g: The holy of holies, entered only by the high priest once a year on the Day of Atonement.

chapters.n: Even the nails were gold-plated, weighing fifty shekels, and the upper rooms were also overlaid with gold.

f.g: About 1.25 pounds (575 g).

chapters.n: Inside the most holy place stood two large carved cherubim, covered with gold, overshadowing the ark.

f.g: Sculpted or carved work.

chapters.n: The cherubim’s wings stretched a total of twenty cubits. One cherub’s outer wing touched the wall while its inner wing touched the other cherub’s wing.
The second cherub mirrored the first: one wing to the opposite wall, the other meeting its partner’s wing in the middle — together spanning the whole room.
The two cherubim stood upright and faced inward toward the main hall, their outspread wings forming a canopy over the ark — the throne of God.

f.g: Literally ‘toward the house,’ i.e. facing the main hall.

chapters.n: A veil of blue, purple, crimson, and fine linen embroidered with cherubim separated the holy place from the most holy place. When Jesus died, the temple veil was torn — opening the way into God’s presence.
Two huge bronze pillars stood before the temple, with decorated capitals on top. (1 Kings gives each pillar’s height as 18 cubits; the 35 here may be their combined length.)

f.g: Capital — the decorated top of a column.

chapters.n: The pillar tops were decorated with chainwork and a hundred pomegranates — symbols of fruitfulness also embroidered on the high priest’s robe.

f.g: ‘Oracle’ (Hebrew devir) usually means the inner sanctuary; here the text may mean ‘like a necklace.’

chapters.n: The pillars were named Jachin (“He will establish”) and Boaz (“In Him is strength”). Their names proclaimed that God would make His house and His people firm and strong.

f.g: Hebrew ‘He establishes’ or ‘He will establish.’
Hebrew ‘in Him is strength’ — also the name of David’s ancestor.

chapters.n: Solomon made a huge bronze altar for burnt offerings, about 30 feet square and 15 feet high — far larger than the tabernacle altar. It stood in the courtyard where the people brought their sacrifices.

f.g: ‘Brass’ in the KJV usually means bronze (copper and tin).

chapters.n: The “molten sea” was a giant cast-bronze basin, about 15 feet across and 7½ feet deep. Its size declared the greatness of God and the importance of being clean before Him.

f.g: A great cast-metal water basin; ‘sea’ suggests its vastness.

chapters.n: Rows of ox figures were cast into the bowl beneath its rim, made in one piece with it. (1 Kings 7:24 describes these as gourds, perhaps a related decorative pattern.)

f.g: Likeness or image.

chapters.n: The sea rested on twelve bronze oxen, three facing each direction. The twelve likely represented the tribes of Israel; Latter-day Saint temple baptismal fonts follow this same pattern.

f.g: Rear ends; the oxen faced outward with their backs toward the center.

chapters.n: The bronze was a hand’s width thick, and its rim curved outward like a cup or lily blossom. It held about 3,000 baths — perhaps 17,000 gallons. (1 Kings gives 2,000 baths, perhaps a different measuring method.)

f.g: About 3 inches (7.5 cm).

chapters.n: Ten smaller basins on wheeled stands were placed on either side for rinsing the sacrificial parts, while the great sea was for the priests’ own washing. Purity was required both of the offering and the one offering.

f.g: Washing basins.

chapters.n: Ten golden lampstands, made to the prescribed pattern, lined the holy place — five on each side — filling the house with light.

f.g: According to the pattern ordained for them.

chapters.n: Ten tables (for the bread of the Presence) were placed in the holy place, and a hundred golden bowls were made, likely for sprinkling sacrificial blood.

f.g: Bowls used for sprinkling or pouring.

chapters.n: Solomon built an inner court for the priests and a larger outer court for the people, with bronze-covered doors between them.

f.g: The inner court, also called the ‘inner court’ in Kings.

chapters.n: The great sea was set at the southeast corner of the temple building.

f.g: Toward the south side.

chapters.n: Huram the craftsman finished the remaining bronze work — pots for removing ashes, shovels, and bowls — completing his assignment for Solomon.
A summary list of Huram’s work: the two pillars with their bowl-shaped capitals and the decorative lattice wreaths covering them.

f.g: Bowl-shaped or rounded parts of the column capitals.
Lattice or network ornaments.

chapters.n: Four hundred pomegranates hung in two rows around each lattice wreath of the pillar capitals.
Huram also made the wheeled stands and the basins that sat upon them.

f.g: Movable bronze stands on wheels.

chapters.n: He made the one great sea and the twelve oxen beneath it.
All the bronze utensils were made of polished bronze by Huram, here honored as “his father” — likely a title of respect meaning master craftsman.

f.g: See 2 Chronicles 2:13; ‘father’ here is probably an honorific.
Polished or burnished bronze.

chapters.n: The large bronze pieces were cast in clay molds in the Jordan valley, where the clay soil was ideal for casting.

f.g: A town east of the Jordan river.
Called Zarethan in 1 Kings 7:46; location near the Jordan.

chapters.n: So much bronze was used that no one even tried to weigh it. The abundance reflects both Solomon’s wealth and David’s preparation.

f.g: Could not be determined or calculated.

chapters.n: Solomon also made the gold furnishings for the interior: the golden incense altar and the tables for the bread of the Presence.
The pure-gold lampstands were to burn before the inner sanctuary as the law required.

f.g: According to the prescribed ordinance.
The inner sanctuary — the most holy place.

chapters.n: Even the decorative flowers, lamps, and tongs were made of the finest gold.

f.g: The purest, completely refined gold.

chapters.n: Wick trimmers, bowls, spoons, and incense pans were pure gold, and the doors to the holy place and most holy place were gold too. Approaching God’s presence meant moving inward toward ever greater holiness.

f.g: Tools to trim lamp wicks.
Pans for carrying burning coals and incense.

chapters.n: With construction complete, Solomon placed in the temple treasury all the silver, gold, and vessels David had dedicated. Father and son together brought the house to completion.

f.w: the things that David his father had dedicated

chapters.n: Solomon gathered the leaders of every tribe to bring the ark up from the City of David — the old Jebusite stronghold of Zion — to the new temple on the higher hill to the north.

f.w: the city of David, which is Zion

chapters.n: The dedication took place during the feast of the seventh month — the Feast of Tabernacles, Israel’s joyful harvest festival.

f.w: the feast which was in the seventh month
f.g: The Feast of Tabernacles (Booths), in the month Ethanim/Tishri.

chapters.n: This time the ark was carried properly by the Levites, as the law required — unlike the earlier attempt with a cart that ended in Uzza’s death.

f.w: the Levites took up the ark

chapters.n: The ark, the old tabernacle tent from Gibeon, and its holy vessels were all brought up together, uniting Israel’s worship in one place.
As the procession moved, the king and people offered so many sheep and cattle that no one could count them — overflowing gratitude.

f.g: Could not be counted.

chapters.n: The priests set the ark in its permanent home: the innermost room, beneath the outstretched wings of the great cherubim.

f.g: To its appointed place.
The inner sanctuary, the most holy place.

chapters.n: The cherubim’s wings formed a canopy over the ark and its carrying poles.

f.g: The carrying poles of the ark.

chapters.n: The poles were drawn forward so their ends could be seen from just outside the inner room, but not from farther away. “Unto this day” shows the Chronicler is copying an older source written while the temple still stood.
Only the two stone tablets of the Ten Commandments were inside the ark. At the heart of the temple was God’s covenant word.

f.g: Another name for Mount Sinai.

chapters.n: All the priests present had purified themselves for this event and served together, not by their usual rotating shifts.

f.g: Ritually purified and set apart.

f.w: did not then wait by course
f.g: Did not keep to their normal assigned divisions.

chapters.n: Levite singers from the families of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun, dressed in white linen, played cymbals, lyres, and harps beside 120 priests blowing trumpets.

f.g: Stringed instruments like lyres or harps.

chapters.n: When musicians and singers praised in perfect unity — “For he is good; for his mercy endureth for ever” — the cloud of God’s presence filled the house. Unity in worship invites God’s presence.

f.w: For he is good; for his mercy endureth for ever

chapters.n: The glory was so overwhelming that the priests could not continue their service. Just as at the tabernacle’s dedication, God accepted this house as His own. Latter-day Saints recall similar outpourings at the Kirtland Temple dedication.

f.w: the glory of the LORD had filled the house

chapters.n: Seeing the cloud, Solomon recalls that God had chosen to reveal Himself in thick darkness — as at Sinai. The cloud shows God is truly present, though veiled.
Solomon presents the temple to God as a permanent dwelling — a fixed home in place of the movable tabernacle.

f.g: A settled dwelling place.

chapters.n: Solomon turns from facing the temple to face the people and pronounces a blessing on them as they stand in respect.
Solomon praises God for keeping with His hands what He promised with His mouth. God’s word and deeds always match.

f.w: with his hands fulfilled that which he spake with his mouth

chapters.n: Solomon recounts God’s words: from the Exodus until David, God had not chosen one city for His temple or one permanent ruling family.

f.w: that my name might be there

chapters.n: But now God has chosen both Jerusalem as the place for His name and David to lead His people.
Solomon reminds the people that building a temple was David’s heartfelt desire.
God commended David for wanting to build the house. Even unfulfilled righteous desires are honored by God.

f.w: thou didst well in that it was in thine heart

chapters.n: Yet the work itself was given to David’s son. God sometimes lets one generation dream and another generation build.

f.g: From your own body — your direct descendant.

chapters.n: Solomon testifies that God has kept every part of His promise: Solomon sits on David’s throne and the temple stands.

f.g: In David’s place; as his successor.

chapters.n: The ark, holding the covenant tablets, now rests in the temple. The covenant is the heart of Israel’s relationship with God.
Solomon stands before the bronze altar in front of everyone and spreads out his hands — the ancient posture of prayer.

Solomon had built a bronze platform in the court. Standing on it, he knelt before all Israel with hands raised to heaven — a king humbling himself before the true King. This detail is unique to Chronicles.

f.g: A bronze platform, about 7½ feet square and 4½ feet high.

chapters.n: The dedicatory prayer begins: no god in heaven or earth is like the Lord, who keeps covenant and shows steadfast love to those who walk before Him wholeheartedly.
Solomon thanks God for keeping His word to David — promised by His mouth and fulfilled by His hand that very day.
Solomon asks God to keep the rest of the promise: David will always have an heir on the throne — on condition that his descendants obey God’s law.

f.w: There shall not fail thee a man

chapters.n: Solomon prays that God’s word to David will be proven true. Christians see its final fulfillment in Jesus, the eternal King from David’s line.
A profound question: can the infinite God really live among people on earth? Even the heavens can’t contain Him, let alone a building. The Gospel answers it: in Jesus, God dwelt among us.

f.w: will God in very deed dwell with men on the earth?

chapters.n: Solomon asks God to give attention to his prayer and pleading.

f.g: Humble, earnest pleading.

chapters.n: He asks that God’s eyes be on this house day and night and that He hear every prayer offered toward it. Ancient Israelites far away prayed facing the temple.
The theme of the whole prayer: when Your people pray here, hear from heaven — and forgive. The temple is above all a place of forgiveness.
The first case: when someone is accused of wronging a neighbor and must swear an oath of innocence before the altar.

f.w: an oath be laid upon him

chapters.n: Solomon asks God to judge justly in such cases — punishing the guilty and vindicating the innocent. God is the ultimate witness of truth.

f.w: recompensing his way upon his own head
f.g: Bringing his own conduct back on him.

chapters.n: Second case: when Israel is defeated in battle because of sin, yet turns back, confesses God, and prays in the temple.

f.g: Defeated.
Acknowledge God openly and His authority.

chapters.n: Then forgive them and bring them back to their land. Restoration follows repentance.

f.w: bring them again unto the land

chapters.n: Third case: drought sent because of sin. Rain in that dry land was life itself, and God had linked it to obedience.
Solomon asks God to forgive, teach His people the right way, and send rain. Forgiveness includes instruction for a better path.
Fourth: every kind of disaster — famine, plague, crop diseases, locusts, siege, or illness.

f.g: Famine; scarcity.
Crop damage from scorching east winds.
Probably a stage of locust.

chapters.n: Whenever anyone, aware of his own sorrow, spreads out his hands toward this house, Solomon asks God to hear. Personal grief, not just national crisis, matters to God.

f.g: Feel his own affliction or the plague of his own heart.

chapters.n: Only God truly knows each heart, so only He can rightly forgive and repay each person according to his ways.
The purpose of God’s mercy is that His people will revere Him and walk in His ways all their lives.

f.g: Revere and honor God with awe.

chapters.n: Remarkably, Solomon also prays for foreigners who come because they’ve heard of God’s greatness. The temple was meant to bless all nations.

f.g: An image of God’s power displayed in delivering His people.

chapters.n: Grant the foreigner’s prayer, Solomon pleads, so that every nation may know and revere God and recognize this house as His.

f.w: that all people of the earth may know thy name

chapters.n: Next, when Israel goes to battle at God’s direction and prays toward Jerusalem and the temple.
Then hear and uphold their cause.

f.g: Secure justice for them; defend their right.

chapters.n: The last and longest case: when Israel sins — and everyone sins — and is carried into exile. Solomon is looking ahead to what would happen in Babylon.

f.w: there is no man which sinneth not

chapters.n: If in captivity they come to their senses and confess, “We have sinned, we have done wrong, we have acted wickedly.” Daniel prayed in this very spirit in Babylon.

f.g: Literally ‘bring back to their heart’ — come to their senses.

chapters.n: If they return to God with all their heart and soul and pray toward their land, city, and temple — full repentance, even far from home.

f.w: with all their heart and with all their soul

chapters.n: Then hear, defend them, and forgive. The Chronicler’s first readers, returned from exile, would have seen this prayer answered in their own story.
Solomon’s closing plea: let Your eyes be open and Your ears attentive to every prayer made here.

f.g: Attentive.

chapters.n: Quoting Psalm 132, Solomon invites God to arise and enter His resting place with the ark. He prays that priests be clothed with salvation and the faithful rejoice in God’s goodness.

f.w: arise, O LORD God, into thy resting place

chapters.n: Finally: do not reject Your anointed king; remember Your steadfast love for David. The prayer ends by resting on God’s covenant faithfulness.

f.g: Hebrew mashiaḥ — the anointed king; the root of the title Messiah.

chapters.n: As soon as Solomon finished praying, fire fell from heaven and consumed the sacrifices, and God’s glory filled the house. Heaven’s fire was God’s visible “yes” to the prayer and the temple.

f.w: the fire came down from heaven

chapters.n: Once again the priests could not enter because of the overwhelming glory. God’s presence, not human effort, made the house holy.

f.w: the glory of the LORD had filled the LORD's house

chapters.n: Seeing the fire and glory, all Israel fell face down on the stone pavement and worshipped, repeating the same refrain sung at the ark’s arrival: “For he is good; for his mercy endureth for ever.”

f.w: For he is good; for his mercy endureth for ever

chapters.n: The king and people respond to God’s glory by offering sacrifices together.
Solomon offered 22,000 cattle and 120,000 sheep — a staggering figure that shows the joy and scale of the dedication.

f.g: Hebrew ḥanak — to inaugurate; related to the later Jewish festival name Hanukkah.

chapters.n: Priests and Levites served in their places with the instruments David had made, praising God’s enduring love, as trumpets sounded and all Israel stood.

f.w: instruments of musick of the LORD, which David the king had made

chapters.n: There were so many offerings that the bronze altar could not hold them all, so Solomon set apart the center of the courtyard as a holy place for additional sacrifices.

f.g: Made holy; consecrated.
Grain offerings (‘meat’ in the KJV means food in general).

chapters.n: Solomon held the festival for seven days with a vast crowd from the far north (the pass of Hamath) to the far south (the brook of Egypt) — the full extent of the promised land.

f.g: Lebo-hamath, the northern border region in Syria.
The Wadi el-Arish, a seasonal stream on the border with Egypt, not the Nile.

chapters.n: Fourteen days of celebration: seven for dedicating the altar and seven for the Feast of Tabernacles, ending with a solemn assembly on the eighth day.

f.g: A sacred gathering marking the end of a festival.

chapters.n: On the twenty-third day of the month, Solomon sent the people home happy and grateful for all the good God had done for David, Solomon, and Israel.
Solomon successfully completed both the temple and his palace — everything he had set his heart to do.

f.g: Successfully accomplished.

chapters.n: Later God appeared to Solomon at night, telling him his prayer was heard and the temple accepted as a house of sacrifice.

f.w: the LORD appeared to Solomon by night

chapters.n: God picks up the scenarios of Solomon’s prayer — drought, locusts, plague — acknowledging that such trials might come as discipline.

One of the most loved promises in scripture: if God’s covenant people humble themselves, pray, seek His face, and turn from evil, He will hear, forgive, and heal their land. It is the Chronicler’s key verse on repentance.

f.w: which are called by my name
f.g: People who bear God’s name by covenant.

chapters.n: God answers Solomon’s exact request: His eyes will be open and His ears attentive to prayers made in this place.
God declares that He has chosen and made holy this house; His name, eyes, and heart will be there continually. The temple is where God’s heart is turned toward His people.

f.w: mine eyes and mine heart shall be there perpetually

chapters.n: God now speaks to Solomon personally: walk before Me as David did, and keep My commandments.

f.g: The Chronicler’s ideal of David is his devotion and repentance, not sinlessness.

chapters.n: If Solomon obeys, God will secure his throne and keep His covenant with David — a ruler will never be lacking.

f.g: Establish; make firm.

chapters.n: But the warning is equally clear: if they turn away and serve other gods, the blessings will be lost. The “ye” widens the warning to all Israel.
Israel would be uprooted from the land and even this glorious temple rejected and mocked by the nations. This happened when Babylon destroyed it in 587 BC.

f.g: An object of ridicule and scorn.

f.w: pluck them up by the roots

chapters.n: Passers-by would be shocked to see such a grand temple in ruins and would ask why the Lord allowed it.

f.g: Something that causes horror and amazement.

chapters.n: The answer would be plain: because they abandoned the God who freed them from Egypt and served other gods. Sacred buildings are no protection without faithful hearts.

f.g: Clung to other gods.

f.w: therefore hath he brought all this evil upon them

chapters.n: After twenty years of building — seven for the temple and thirteen for his palace — Solomon turned to other projects across his kingdom.
Solomon rebuilt cities that Huram had given (or returned) to him and settled Israelites there. 1 Kings says Solomon gave Hiram twenty cities; perhaps Hiram, displeased, gave them back.

f.w: the cities which Huram had restored to Solomon

chapters.n: Solomon conquered Hamath-zobah, an area in Syria — his only recorded military campaign.

f.g: A region of Aramean (Syrian) territory north of Israel.

chapters.n: He built Tadmor, a desert oasis on the trade routes, and store cities in the Hamath region to secure trade and supplies.

f.g: Later known as Palmyra, an oasis in the Syrian desert.
Towns for storing grain, supplies, and equipment.

chapters.n: Solomon fortified Upper and Lower Beth-horon, guarding a key pass from the coast up to Jerusalem.

f.g: Fortified, walled cities.
Heavy bolts to secure the gates.

chapters.n: He also built Baalath, more store and chariot cities, and whatever else he wanted in Jerusalem, Lebanon, and throughout his realm.
The Chronicler names the remnants of Canaan’s earlier inhabitants still living in the land.

f.w: the Hittites, and the Amorites, and the Perizzites, and the Hivites, and the Jebusites

chapters.n: Solomon conscripted these remaining non-Israelite peoples into forced labor, which continued to the Chronicler’s source’s time.

f.g: Did not completely destroy.
Here, compulsory labor service.

chapters.n: Israelites were not made slaves; they served as soldiers, commanders, and officers. (1 Kings 5 does record Israelites being drafted for rotating labor, which later caused resentment.)

f.w: of the children of Israel did Solomon make no servants

chapters.n: Two hundred fifty chief officials supervised the work and the workers.

f.g: Exercised authority; supervised.

chapters.n: Solomon moved his Egyptian wife, Pharaoh’s daughter, out of David’s palace because places where the ark had been were holy. This hints at tension: a foreign, likely idolatrous wife near holy things.
Solomon offered burnt offerings on the Lord’s altar in front of the temple porch.
He followed Moses’ law exactly: daily offerings, Sabbath and new-moon offerings, and the three yearly pilgrim festivals — Unleavened Bread (Passover), Weeks (Pentecost), and Tabernacles.

f.w: after a certain rate every day
f.g: According to the daily requirement.

chapters.n: He also organized priests, Levites, and gatekeepers in their rotating divisions, exactly as David had ordained. The Chronicler loves to show worship done in order.

f.g: Gatekeepers of the temple.
A title usually given to prophets; here it honors David’s inspired arrangements.

chapters.n: The priests and Levites followed the king’s instructions faithfully in every matter, including the treasuries.
All Solomon’s work, from laying the foundation to completion, was carried out, and the temple was finished.

f.g: Completed.

chapters.n: Solomon went to the Red Sea ports of Ezion-geber and Eloth (Elath) in Edom’s territory.

f.g: A port at the northern tip of the Gulf of Aqaba.

chapters.n: Huram sent ships and skilled Phoenician sailors who, together with Solomon’s men, sailed to Ophir and brought back 450 talents of gold — over 15 tons.
Hearing of Solomon’s fame, the queen of Sheba traveled to Jerusalem with a great caravan to test him with difficult questions and riddles, and she shared everything on her mind.

f.g: A wealthy trading kingdom, most likely in southwest Arabia (modern Yemen).
Test.

chapters.n: Solomon answered every question; nothing was too hard for him to explain.

f.g: Answered all her questions.

chapters.n: The queen observed both Solomon’s wisdom and the palace he had built.
The food, the seating of his officials, the service of attendants, their clothing, and the ascent he made to the temple left her breathless with wonder.

f.g: The food served at his table.

f.w: there was no more spirit in her
f.g: She was overwhelmed — it took her breath away.
Could also be read ‘his burnt offerings’ — the sacrifices he offered.

chapters.n: She tells Solomon that the reports she heard back home were true.
She hadn’t believed them until she saw for herself — and the reality was even greater than the reports. Firsthand experience surpasses hearsay.
She declares Solomon’s servants fortunate to hear his wisdom daily.

f.g: Blessed; fortunate.

chapters.n: This foreign queen praises Solomon’s God, recognizing that Solomon sits on God’s throne and rules for Him, to bring justice. In Chronicles the throne belongs to God.
She gave Solomon 120 talents of gold (about four tons), vast quantities of spices, and precious stones. No one had seen spices like hers.
Huram’s and Solomon’s sailors also brought algum wood and gems from Ophir.
Solomon used the algum wood for steps or walkways in the temple and palace and to make harps and lyres for the singers — instruments unlike any seen before in Judah.

f.g: Possibly steps, railings, or supports; the Hebrew word is uncertain.
Stringed instruments.

chapters.n: Solomon gave the queen everything she asked for — more than she had brought — and she returned home.
Solomon’s yearly income in gold was 666 talents — about 25 tons. The number simply records his immense wealth.

f.w: six hundred and threescore and six talents

chapters.n: Beyond this, traders, merchants, Arabian kings, and regional governors brought him gold and silver.

f.g: Traveling traders; peddlers.

chapters.n: Solomon made 200 large shields of hammered gold, each containing 600 shekels of gold (about 15 pounds).

f.g: Large body-length shields.
Hammered gold.

chapters.n: He also made 300 smaller gold shields and displayed them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon. These shields would later be carried off by Egypt.

f.w: the house of the forest of Lebanon
f.g: A large hall in Solomon’s palace built with many cedar pillars.

chapters.n: Solomon made a magnificent throne of ivory covered with pure gold.
The throne had six steps, a golden footstool attached to it, armrests on both sides, and two lions standing beside the armrests.

f.g: Armrests.
Lions were symbols of royal power — and of Judah.

chapters.n: Twelve lions stood on the steps, one on each end of the six steps. No other kingdom had anything like it.
All Solomon’s cups and the vessels of his great hall were of pure gold. Silver was so common that it was considered almost worthless.

f.w: it was not any thing accounted of
f.g: It was not valued at all.

chapters.n: Solomon’s fleet, with Huram’s sailors, made voyages every three years, bringing back gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks (or baboons).

f.g: ‘Ships of Tarshish’ were large ocean-going vessels; Tarshish itself may have been in Spain.
Possibly peacocks or baboons; the Hebrew word is uncertain.

chapters.n: Solomon surpassed every king on earth in wealth and wisdom — the high point of Israel’s glory.

f.w: passed all the kings of the earth

chapters.n: Kings everywhere wanted to meet Solomon and hear the wisdom God had put in his heart. The source of his wisdom is God.

f.w: that God had put in his heart

chapters.n: Visitors brought yearly gifts: silver and gold vessels, clothing, weapons, spices, horses, and mules.

f.g: Armor or weapons.
A set amount each year.

chapters.n: Solomon had 4,000 stalls for horses and chariots and 12,000 horsemen, stationed in chariot cities and in Jerusalem.
He ruled over the kings from the Euphrates to the land of the Philistines and to Egypt’s border — fulfilling the boundaries promised to Abraham.

f.g: The Euphrates River.

chapters.n: Silver became as common as stones in Jerusalem, and cedar as plentiful as sycamore-figs.
Horses were brought to Solomon from Egypt and many other lands. The repeated emphasis on horses and gold quietly echoes the warnings for kings in Deuteronomy.
For more about Solomon, the Chronicler points to prophetic records by Nathan, Ahijah of Shiloh, and Iddo. Notably, Chronicles omits Solomon’s later turn to idolatry told in 1 Kings 11.
Solomon reigned forty years over all Israel, from about 970 to 930 BC.
Solomon died and was buried in the City of David. His son Rehoboam became king — and the united kingdom was about to split.

f.g: A gentle idiom for death, implying joining one’s ancestors.

chapters.n: Rehoboam goes to Shechem, an ancient center of the northern tribes, where all Israel has gathered to confirm him as king. His acceptance there was not automatic.

f.g: An old covenant site in the hill country of Ephraim, where Joshua renewed Israel’s covenant.

chapters.n: Jeroboam, a former official of Solomon who had fled to Egypt after a prophet promised him ten tribes, hears the news and comes back.
The people call Jeroboam to be their spokesman, and together they approach Rehoboam.
Their request is reasonable: Solomon’s taxes and forced labor were crushing. Lighten the load, and we will serve you.

f.g: A wooden bar on oxen — here a picture of heavy taxes and labor.
Heavy, hard to bear.

chapters.n: Rehoboam asks for three days to think it over.
First he consults the older advisers who had served Solomon — men of experience.

f.g: Served as officials or attendants.

chapters.n: Their counsel: be kind, serve the people, and speak gently, and they will be loyal forever. Servant leadership wins hearts.

f.w: If thou be kind to this people

chapters.n: Rehoboam rejects this wise advice and turns to the young men who had grown up with him in privilege.
He asks his peers how to answer the people’s request for relief.
His friends urge a boastful reply: “My little finger is thicker than my father’s waist” — meaning my weakest effort will be harsher than his strongest.

f.g: Waist or hips.

chapters.n: They suggest he threaten even heavier burdens: Solomon used whips, but Rehoboam will use “scorpions” — possibly barbed whips that stung like scorpions.

f.g: Probably whips with metal barbs or knots, named for their sting.

chapters.n: On the third day Jeroboam and the people return as instructed.
Rehoboam speaks harshly, disregarding the elders’ wise counsel.

f.g: Harshly.

chapters.n: He repeats the young men’s threats word for word. Pride and inexperience cost him most of his kingdom.

f.g: I will make it even heavier.

chapters.n: Behind Rehoboam’s foolishness, God’s purposes were at work. Ahijah had prophesied that ten tribes would be torn from Solomon’s house because of Solomon’s idolatry.

f.g: The turn of events came from God — not excusing Rehoboam, but fulfilling prophecy.

chapters.n: The northern tribes reject David’s dynasty with a rallying cry: “We have no share in David — go home, Israel! David, look after your own house.” The united kingdom splits in two.

f.w: What portion have we in David?

f.g: Go home — an old call to disband.

chapters.n: Only the Israelites living in Judah’s towns remained under Rehoboam. From now on “Judah” is the southern kingdom and “Israel” usually the northern.
Rehoboam foolishly sent Hadoram, the very official in charge of forced labor, to negotiate. The people stoned him to death, and Rehoboam barely escaped to Jerusalem in his chariot.

f.g: Called Adoram or Adoniram in Kings.
Forced labor.

chapters.n: The split between north and south continued from then on. The prophets later looked ahead to a day when Judah and Israel would be one again.
Back in Jerusalem, Rehoboam musters 180,000 soldiers from Judah and Benjamin to win back the northern tribes by force.

f.g: The two tribes that stayed loyal to David’s house (along with most priests and Levites).

chapters.n: God speaks to a prophet named Shemaiah.
Shemaiah is to deliver God’s message to the king and all the people of Judah and Benjamin.
God forbids civil war: do not fight your own brothers, because this division is My doing. Remarkably, Rehoboam and his army listen and go home.

f.g: The northern tribes were still kin — fellow descendants of Jacob.

f.w: this thing is done of me

chapters.n: Instead of attacking the north, Rehoboam strengthens Judah’s defenses by fortifying towns.

f.g: Fortified towns.

chapters.n: The list of fortified towns begins with Bethlehem (David’s hometown), Etam, and Tekoa (later the home of the prophet Amos) — all south of Jerusalem.
More towns: Beth-zur, Socoh, and Adullam — forts in the hills and western foothills. Adullam was where David once hid in a cave.
Gath (once a Philistine city), Mareshah, and Ziph complete the southwestern line of defense.

f.g: Goliath’s hometown, at this time apparently under Judah’s control.

chapters.n: Adoraim, Lachish, and Azekah guarded the southwest approaches. Lachish became one of Judah’s most important fortresses.
Zorah, Aijalon, and Hebron complete the list. Most of these forts faced west and south, suggesting Rehoboam feared Egypt and the coastlands more than Israel.

f.g: Samson’s hometown.

chapters.n: He strengthened the fortresses, posted commanders, and stocked them with food, oil, and wine to withstand sieges.

f.g: Food supplies.

chapters.n: Each city was armed with shields and spears and made very strong, keeping Judah and Benjamin secure.

f.g: Each individual city.

chapters.n: Priests and Levites from all over the north came to support Rehoboam. True worshippers gathered where true worship continued.

f.g: Territories or borders (not seashores).

chapters.n: The Levites left their homes and lands in the north because Jeroboam had barred them from serving as priests of the Lord. They chose faith over property.

f.g: Pasture lands around the Levitical towns.

chapters.n: Jeroboam appointed his own priests for the hill shrines, for goat-idols, and for the golden calves he had made at Bethel and Dan.

f.g: Hebrew se‘irim — goat-demons or goat idols.

f.w: the calves which he had made

chapters.n: Faithful people from every tribe who set their hearts to seek the Lord also came to Jerusalem to worship. The southern kingdom thus kept members of all twelve tribes.

f.w: set their hearts to seek the LORD

chapters.n: These faithful newcomers strengthened Judah for three years, while the kingdom followed the ways of David and Solomon. Faithfulness is the real strength of a nation.
Rehoboam married Mahalath, a granddaughter of David, and Abihail, a descendant of David’s brother Eliab. These marriages kept power within the royal family.
Mahalath bore him three sons: Jeush, Shamariah, and Zaham.
He also married Maachah, a descendant (probably granddaughter) of David’s rebellious son Absalom. Her son Abijah would become the next king.

f.g: ‘Daughter’ can mean granddaughter; see 2 Chronicles 13:2.

chapters.n: Rehoboam loved Maachah most among his eighteen wives and sixty concubines, and had eighty-eight children. Kings were forbidden to multiply wives, but royal custom often ignored that.

f.g: Secondary wives with lower status.

chapters.n: He made Maachah’s son Abijah chief prince among his brothers, intending him to be king.
Shrewdly, Rehoboam spread his sons out among the fortified cities, giving them provisions and wives. This kept them busy and loyal and avoided rivalry at the capital.

f.g: Acted shrewdly or prudently.
Or ‘he sought many wives for them’ — for his sons.

chapters.n: Once Rehoboam felt secure and strong, he abandoned God’s law, and the people followed. Success and security often tempt people to forget God — a pattern the Book of Mormon calls the pride cycle.

f.w: he forsook the law of the LORD

chapters.n: In Rehoboam’s fifth year (about 925 BC), Shishak of Egypt invaded. The Chronicler states the spiritual cause plainly: they had been unfaithful to the Lord.

f.g: Pharaoh Shoshenq I, whose victory inscription at Karnak in Egypt lists towns in Israel and Judah.

chapters.n: Shishak came with 1,200 chariots, 60,000 horsemen, and countless troops, including Libyans, Sukkiim, and Ethiopians (Cushites).

f.g: Libyans.
Possibly a group of foreign troops serving Egypt; identity uncertain.
Cushites, from the upper Nile region (modern Sudan).

chapters.n: He captured Judah’s fortified cities — the very forts Rehoboam had built — and reached Jerusalem. Walls are no substitute for faith.
The prophet Shemaiah tells the king and leaders plainly: You abandoned Me, so I have abandoned you to Shishak.

f.w: Ye have forsaken me, and therefore have I also left you

chapters.n: The king and princes humble themselves and admit, “The LORD is righteous” — accepting that the punishment is just.
Because they humbled themselves, God spares them from destruction and grants partial deliverance. Humility immediately changes God’s response — a central theme in Chronicles.
Still, they will serve Shishak for a time, so they learn the difference between serving God and serving earthly kings.

f.w: that they may know my service, and the service of the kingdoms

chapters.n: Shishak carried off the treasures of the temple and palace, including Solomon’s famous gold shields. Within five years of Solomon’s death, much of his glory was gone.

f.w: the shields of gold which Solomon had made

chapters.n: Rehoboam replaced them with bronze shields — a sad picture of decline: bronze in place of gold, appearances maintained while true glory faded.

f.g: Shields of bronze.

chapters.n: Whenever the king went to the temple, the guards carried out the bronze shields for ceremony and then returned them to the guardroom.

f.g: The armory of the royal guards.

chapters.n: Because he humbled himself, God’s anger turned away and Judah was not completely destroyed; some good things remained in the land.

f.g: Or ‘there were good things in Judah’ — some faithfulness remained.

chapters.n: Rehoboam regained strength and reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem, God’s chosen city. He became king at forty-one; his mother Naamah was an Ammonite.

f.w: the city which the LORD had chosen

chapters.n: The summary of his reign: he did evil because he didn’t set his heart to seek the Lord. A heart not deliberately prepared for God drifts into sin.

f.w: he prepared not his heart to seek the LORD

chapters.n: Rehoboam’s deeds were recorded by the prophet Shemaiah and Iddo the seer. Fighting between Rehoboam and Jeroboam never stopped.

f.g: Referring to genealogical records.

chapters.n: Rehoboam died and was buried in the City of David; his son Abijah succeeded him.

f.g: Called Abijam in 1 Kings.

chapters.n: Abijah began to rule Judah in the eighteenth year of Jeroboam’s reign over Israel. Chronicles dates southern kings by northern ones only here.
Abijah reigned three years. His mother is named Michaiah daughter of Uriel; elsewhere she is called Maachah, probably a variant name. War with Jeroboam continued.

f.g: Elsewhere called Maachah, granddaughter of Absalom; the names may be variants.

chapters.n: Abijah gathered 400,000 elite soldiers; Jeroboam came with 800,000. Judah was outnumbered two to one. The huge numbers may reflect military units rather than exact head counts.

f.g: Lined up the troops for battle.

chapters.n: Before battle, Abijah stood on Mount Zemaraim in Ephraim’s hill country and called out to Jeroboam and the northern army.

f.g: A hill near the border between Judah and Israel, probably near Bethel.

chapters.n: Abijah reminds them that God gave the kingdom to David’s family forever by a “covenant of salt” — a permanent, unbreakable covenant.

f.g: Salt preserves and doesn’t decay; a ‘salt covenant’ is permanent and binding.

chapters.n: He accuses Jeroboam, once merely Solomon’s servant, of rebelling against his rightful master.
Worthless troublemakers gathered around Jeroboam and took advantage of Rehoboam, who was then inexperienced and timid.

f.g: Empty, worthless men.
Hebrew idiom for wicked, worthless people (‘sons of worthlessness’).
Here, faint-hearted or inexperienced.

chapters.n: Abijah warns that they are fighting not just Judah but “the kingdom of the LORD” held by David’s sons. Their large numbers and golden calves cannot save them.
They drove out the true priests and made anyone who brought a bull and seven rams into a priest of non-gods. Priesthood had become something you could buy.

f.g: Literally ‘fill his hand’ — to be ordained.

f.w: the priests of the LORD, the sons of Aaron

chapters.n: In contrast, Judah has not forsaken the Lord: their priests are Aaron’s descendants, assisted by the Levites. Authority to act for God matters.
Judah keeps the daily sacrifices, incense, bread of the Presence, and the golden lampstand as the law commands. You have forsaken Him; we keep His charge.

f.g: The gold table of the bread of the Presence.

f.w: we keep the charge of the LORD
f.g: We faithfully perform the duties God assigned.

chapters.n: God Himself leads Judah, with priests ready to sound the battle trumpets. Abijah pleads: don’t fight against the God of your fathers — you cannot win.
While Abijah spoke, Jeroboam sent troops around behind Judah to set an ambush, trapping them from front and rear.

f.g: An ambush.

chapters.n: Surrounded, Judah cried out to the Lord, and the priests blew the trumpets.
Judah raised a battle shout, and as they shouted, God struck down Jeroboam and his army. The victory is credited entirely to God.
Israel’s army fled, and God gave them into Judah’s hands.
Israel suffered massive losses. The enormous number underscores how completely the rebellion against God’s chosen house was defeated.
The key lesson: Judah prevailed because they relied on the Lord. In Chronicles, trust in God decides battles.
Abijah captured Bethel — site of one of Jeroboam’s golden calves — along with Jeshanah and Ephron and their villages.

f.g: Probably Ephron or Ophrah, a town north of Jerusalem.

chapters.n: Jeroboam never recovered during Abijah’s reign, and the Lord struck him and he died.
Abijah grew powerful and had a large family: fourteen wives, twenty-two sons, and sixteen daughters.

f.g: Grew strong.

chapters.n: Abijah’s other deeds and speeches are recorded in a work by the prophet Iddo. 1 Kings is less favorable to him, saying his heart was not fully devoted to God.

f.g: Hebrew midrash — a study, commentary, or written account.

chapters.n: Abijah died and his son Asa became king. Asa’s reign began with ten years of peace — in Chronicles, a sign of God’s blessing on faithfulness.

f.w: the land was quiet ten years

chapters.n: Asa did what was good and right in God’s eyes — the Chronicler’s highest praise for a king.
He removed foreign altars and hill shrines, smashed sacred pillars, and cut down Asherah poles — cleaning out the idolatry that had crept in under earlier kings.

f.g: Standing stone pillars used in Canaanite worship.
Hebrew asherim — wooden poles or images honoring the goddess Asherah.

chapters.n: Reform was not only removing evil but commanding good: Asa called Judah to seek the Lord and keep His law.

f.g: A key phrase in Chronicles: to turn to God in worship, prayer, and obedience.

chapters.n: He removed the high places and incense altars from every city, and the kingdom enjoyed peace under him.

f.g: Probably incense altars (Hebrew hammanim).

chapters.n: Asa used the years of peace to fortify cities. God gave rest, and Asa used rest wisely to prepare.

f.w: the LORD had given him rest

chapters.n: Asa told Judah to build while the land was still theirs, testifying that their peace came from seeking God. Prosperity is a time to prepare, not to relax.

f.w: while the land is yet before us
f.g: While the land is still open to us and under our control.

f.w: we have sought him, and he hath given us rest

chapters.n: Asa’s army was large: 300,000 from Judah with large shields and spears, and 280,000 Benjamite archers with small shields.

f.g: Large shields.

chapters.n: Zerah the Cushite invaded with a massive army of “a thousand thousand” — a way of saying an overwhelming host — and 300 chariots, reaching Mareshah in Judah’s foothills.

f.g: A Cushite commander, possibly serving Egypt or ruling Cushite settlers in the south; his exact identity is debated.
A million — likely a round figure meaning a vast, countless army.

chapters.n: Asa went out to meet him and set up battle lines in the Zephathah valley near Mareshah.
Asa’s prayer is a classic of faith: Lord, it makes no difference to You whether those You help are strong or weak. We rely on You and go in Your name; don’t let mere man win against You.

f.w: it is nothing with thee to help

chapters.n: The Lord struck the Cushite army before Asa and Judah, and they fled. The battle is credited to God.
Judah chased them to Gerar in the southwest. The invaders were crushed “before the LORD, and before his host,” and Judah took a great deal of plunder.

f.g: A town in the western Negev, near Gaza.
God’s army — Judah fighting as the Lord’s troops.

chapters.n: Judah also defeated the towns around Gerar, which were terrified by the Lord, and took much plunder from them.

f.w: the fear of the LORD came upon them

chapters.n: They attacked the herdsmen’s camps, took many sheep and camels, and returned to Jerusalem. Some of this spoil was offered to the Lord in the next chapter.

f.g: Encampments of herdsmen.

chapters.n: After the victory, the Spirit of God came upon a prophet named Azariah son of Oded, mentioned only here.

f.w: the Spirit of God came upon

chapters.n: Azariah’s message is the heart of Chronicles: God is with you as long as you are with Him. Seek Him and you will find Him; abandon Him and He will abandon you.

f.w: The LORD is with you, while ye be with him
if ye seek him, he will be found of you

chapters.n: Azariah recalls a dark era — probably the time of the judges — when Israel lived without the true God, without priests who taught, and without the law.
Yet whenever they turned back to God in their distress and sought Him, He let Himself be found. God’s door is open to the repentant.
In those times no one could travel safely; turmoil troubled everyone in the land.

f.w: him that went out, nor to him that came in
f.g: Anyone traveling or going about daily life.
Turmoil and distress.

chapters.n: Nations and cities crushed one another, because God troubled them with every kind of distress — the natural fruit of forsaking Him.
So be strong and don’t lose heart, for your work will be rewarded. The same words appear in God’s promise that faithful labor is never wasted.
Encouraged by the prophecy, Asa removed the idols from Judah, Benjamin, and captured towns in Ephraim, and repaired the Lord’s altar before the temple porch.

f.w: the prophecy of Oded the prophet
f.g: The Hebrew here may have lost ‘Azariah son of’; the prophecy is Azariah’s (v.1).
Detestable things — a strong term for idols.

chapters.n: Asa gathered Judah and Benjamin along with many from Ephraim, Manasseh, and Simeon who defected from the north when they saw God was with him. Faithfulness draws people.

f.g: They came over to his side; defected to him.

chapters.n: They assembled at Jerusalem in the third month of Asa’s fifteenth year — the time of the Feast of Weeks (Pentecost), which celebrated covenant and harvest.

f.g: The month of the Feast of Weeks (Shavuot), traditionally linked with the giving of the law at Sinai.

chapters.n: They offered 700 cattle and 7,000 sheep from the spoil taken in the war against Zerah.

f.w: of the spoil which they had brought

chapters.n: The people made a covenant to seek the Lord with all their heart and soul — echoing the great commandment.

f.w: with all their heart and with all their soul

chapters.n: The covenant included the law’s severe penalty for those who turned to idols. Under the old covenant, Israel enforced idolatry as a capital crime against the nation’s covenant.
They swore their oath loudly, with shouts, trumpets, and rams’ horns — an exuberant public commitment.

f.g: Hebrew shofar — a ram’s-horn trumpet.

chapters.n: All Judah rejoiced over the oath because they made it wholeheartedly. They sought Him with all their desire, He was found, and He gave them rest all around.

Asa even removed his own grandmother Maachah from her role as queen mother because she had made an obscene Asherah image. He destroyed it and burned it in the Kidron Valley. Faith came before family politics.

f.g: ‘Mother’ here likely means grandmother; she was Abijah’s mother (11:20). She held the honored title of queen mother.
The valley east of Jerusalem, where reformers destroyed idols.

chapters.n: Some high places were not removed — perhaps in the northern towns — but Asa’s heart was fully devoted to God all his life (at least in intention).

f.w: the high places were not taken away

chapters.n: Asa brought into the temple the silver, gold, and vessels that he and his father had dedicated to God.
There was no war until Asa’s thirty-fifth year. (The dates in this section are hard to reconcile with Kings; some scholars think they count from the division of the kingdom.)

f.g: Possibly counting from the split of the kingdom, since 1 Kings 16:8 suggests Baasha died earlier in Asa’s reign.

chapters.n: Baasha, king of Israel, fortified Ramah, just five miles north of Jerusalem, to blockade Judah and stop people from crossing over to Asa.

f.g: A town on the main road north of Jerusalem.

chapters.n: Instead of praying as he had against Zerah, Asa took silver and gold from the temple and palace treasuries and sent them to Ben-hadad, king of Syria in Damascus.
Asa asked Ben-hadad to break his treaty with Israel and ally with Judah instead, so Baasha would be forced to withdraw.

f.g: A treaty or alliance.

chapters.n: Ben-hadad agreed and attacked Israel’s northern towns — Ijon, Dan, Abel-maim, and Naphtali’s supply cities.

f.g: Also called Abel-beth-maachah, in the far north.

chapters.n: Hearing this, Baasha stopped building Ramah. Asa’s plan seemed to work — on the surface.
Asa had Judah haul away Ramah’s stones and timber to fortify Geba and Mizpah for Judah’s own defense.

f.g: Border towns of Benjamin.

chapters.n: The seer Hanani rebuked Asa: because you relied on Syria instead of the Lord, you lost the chance to defeat Syria too.

f.g: Father of the prophet Jehu.

chapters.n: Hanani reminds Asa of his own past: when you faced the huge Cushite and Libyan armies and trusted the Lord, He gave you victory. Why trust a pagan king now?
A beloved verse: God’s eyes search the whole earth to show His strength for those whose hearts are fully His. Asa acted foolishly, so from now on he would have wars.

f.w: the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth

f.g: Whole, undivided, completely loyal.

chapters.n: Instead of repenting, Asa became furious, threw the prophet into prison (literally into the stocks), and mistreated some of the people. Pride turned a good king harsh.

f.g: Literally ‘house of the stocks’ — a place of confinement and torture.
Crushed or mistreated.

chapters.n: Asa’s full history was recorded in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel.
In his thirty-ninth year Asa developed a severe foot disease. Even then he sought only doctors, not the Lord. The point is not that medicine is wrong, but that he left God out entirely.

f.g: Possibly healers who used magical or pagan practices, as well as ordinary doctors.

f.w: he sought not to the LORD

chapters.n: Asa died in his forty-first year as king.
He was buried in a tomb he had prepared in the City of David, laid on a bier filled with spices and perfumes, and honored with a great memorial fire (not cremation).

f.g: The skill of perfume makers.
A large ceremonial fire of spices in his honor.

chapters.n: Asa’s son Jehoshaphat became king and strengthened Judah’s defenses against Israel.

f.g: Name means ‘the LORD judges’ — fitting for his later reform of the courts.

chapters.n: He stationed troops in Judah’s fortified cities and in the Ephraimite towns Asa had captured.

f.g: Military outposts or governors.

chapters.n: The Lord was with Jehoshaphat because he followed the early example of David and did not seek the Baals.

f.w: the first ways of his father David
f.g: David’s earlier, faithful years (some manuscripts lack ‘David,’ pointing to Asa’s early ways).
Plural of Baal — the Canaanite storm and fertility gods.

chapters.n: He sought the God of his fathers and obeyed His commands, not the practices of the northern kingdom.

f.g: The calf worship and Baal worship of the northern kingdom.

chapters.n: So God firmly established the kingdom under him. The people brought gifts, and he gained great wealth and honor.

f.g: Gifts or tribute offered to the king.

chapters.n: His heart was “lifted up” — not in pride, but in courage and devotion to the ways of the Lord. He removed high places and Asherah poles.

f.g: Here a good sense: he was encouraged and emboldened in God’s ways.
Asherah poles.

chapters.n: In his third year Jehoshaphat sent officials to teach throughout Judah’s towns. Real reform requires teaching, not just tearing down idols.

f.w: to teach in the cities of Judah

chapters.n: Levites and priests went with the officials. Teaching was a shared effort of civic and religious leaders.
They carried the book of the law and taught people in every town. Scripture-based teaching is the foundation of lasting faith.

f.w: the book of the law of the LORD

chapters.n: The fear of the Lord fell on surrounding kingdoms so that none attacked Judah. Teaching God’s law brought national peace.

f.w: the fear of the LORD fell upon all the kingdoms

chapters.n: Even the Philistines brought gifts and silver, and Arabians brought 7,700 rams and 7,700 goats.

f.g: Silver paid as tribute.

chapters.n: Jehoshaphat became very powerful and built fortresses and storage cities across Judah.

f.g: Fortresses or citadels.

chapters.n: He had extensive supplies in Judah’s towns and experienced soldiers in Jerusalem.

f.g: Possibly ‘supplies’ or ‘works’ — stores and projects.

chapters.n: His army was organized by family clans. Adnah commanded the largest Judahite division.

f.g: Ancestral family groups.

chapters.n: Next was Jehohanan, with another large division.
Amasiah son of Zichri is singled out as one who willingly offered himself to the Lord — a volunteer for God’s service.

f.w: willingly offered himself unto the LORD

chapters.n: From Benjamin, Eliada led archers and shield-bearers.
Next to him Jehozabad commanded troops ready for battle.
These commanders served the king in Jerusalem, besides those stationed in the fortified cities. The large figures, like others in Chronicles, may count military units rather than individuals.

f.g: Served under the king’s direct command.

chapters.n: Despite his wealth and honor, Jehoshaphat formed a marriage alliance with wicked King Ahab of Israel — his son Jehoram married Ahab’s daughter Athaliah. This alliance would later nearly destroy David’s line.

f.g: Made a marriage alliance.

chapters.n: Years later Jehoshaphat visited Ahab in Samaria. Ahab threw him a lavish feast and urged him to join an attack on Ramoth-gilead, a city east of the Jordan held by Syria.

f.g: A fortified town in Gilead, east of the Jordan, disputed between Israel and Syria.
Enticed or lured — the same Hebrew word used for ‘entice’ in v.19-21.

chapters.n: Jehoshaphat agreed: “I am as you are, my people as your people.” Too quickly he tied himself to an ungodly ally.
To his credit, Jehoshaphat insisted that they first ask the Lord what to do.

f.w: Inquire, I pray thee, at the word of the LORD

chapters.n: Ahab gathered 400 court prophets, who unanimously said, “Go — God will give it to you.” They told the king what he wanted to hear.

f.g: Hold back; refrain.

chapters.n: Jehoshaphat sensed something was wrong and asked whether there was a true prophet of the Lord they could consult.

f.w: a prophet of the LORD besides
f.g: Another prophet — one truly of the Lord.

chapters.n: Ahab admits there is one, Micaiah, but says he hates him because he never prophesies anything good for him. Jehoshaphat gently rebukes him.
Ahab sends an officer to bring Micaiah quickly.

f.g: Literally ‘eunuch’ or court official.

chapters.n: The two kings sit in royal robes on thrones at the threshing floor by Samaria’s gate, while the prophets perform before them — an impressive public stage.

f.g: An open space — literally a threshing floor.

chapters.n: Zedekiah, one of the court prophets, makes iron horns as a dramatic sign: with these you will gore Syria to destruction.

f.g: Horns symbolized strength in battle.

chapters.n: All the prophets echo the same message: go up and succeed.
The messenger pressures Micaiah to agree with the others: everyone is saying good things — please do the same.

f.g: Unanimously; with one voice.

chapters.n: Micaiah’s answer is the mark of a true prophet: as the Lord lives, I will speak only what my God says.

f.w: what my God saith, that will I speak

chapters.n: When asked, Micaiah at first sarcastically repeats the false prophets’ words — go up and win. His tone must have made his mockery obvious.
Ahab sees through it and demands the truth in the Lord’s name. Ironically, he knows the truth when he hears it but refuses to obey it.

f.g: Solemnly charge under oath.

chapters.n: Micaiah’s true vision: Israel scattered on the mountains like sheep without a shepherd — meaning their king would die. Jesus later used this image for people without spiritual leadership.

f.w: as sheep that have no shepherd

chapters.n: Ahab turns to Jehoshaphat: “Didn’t I tell you he only predicts disaster for me?”
Micaiah describes a vision of God’s heavenly council: the Lord on His throne, surrounded by the hosts of heaven. True prophets testify of what they have seen in God’s council.

f.w: I saw the LORD sitting upon his throne

f.g: God’s angelic armies and council.

chapters.n: In the vision, the Lord asks who will lure Ahab into battle where he will fall. Various suggestions are made.

f.g: Persuade or lure.

chapters.n: A spirit steps forward and offers to entice Ahab. The Lord asks how.

The spirit says it will be a lying spirit in the prophets’ mouths. The vision depicts God allowing Ahab’s chosen deception to lead him to the judgment he had earned — Ahab wanted lies and received them.

f.w: a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets
f.g: A vivid prophetic picture; scripture elsewhere teaches God does not lie but permits those who reject truth to believe falsehood.

chapters.n: Micaiah applies the vision: your prophets are deceived, and the Lord has decreed disaster for you.
Zedekiah slaps Micaiah and sneers: “Which way did the Spirit of the Lord go from me to talk to you?”
Micaiah replies that Zedekiah will find out when he hides in an inner room on the day disaster strikes.

f.g: A back room — a place to hide in fear.

chapters.n: Ahab orders Micaiah taken to the city governor Amon and to Joash the king’s son.
He commands that Micaiah be imprisoned on minimal bread and water until Ahab returns safely.

f.g: Prison rations — barely enough to survive.

chapters.n: Micaiah stakes his credibility: if you return safely, the Lord has not spoken through me. He calls all the people to witness. This is the biblical test of a prophet.

f.w: then hath not the LORD spoken by me

chapters.n: Despite the warning, both kings go up to Ramoth-gilead.
Ahab tries to outwit the prophecy by disguising himself as an ordinary soldier, while Jehoshaphat wears his royal robes — making Jehoshaphat the obvious target.
The Syrian king had ordered his chariot commanders to target only Israel’s king.

f.g: Anyone, of low or high rank.

chapters.n: Seeing Jehoshaphat’s robes, the Syrians surround him, thinking he is Ahab. Jehoshaphat cries out, and the Lord helps him by turning them away. Chronicles adds that God moved them.
Realizing he wasn’t Israel’s king, the commanders stopped pursuing him.
A soldier shot an arrow at random, and it struck Ahab through a gap in his armor. No disguise can hide anyone from God’s word.

f.g: At random, without a particular aim.
A gap between plates of the armor.

chapters.n: As the battle raged, Ahab was propped up in his chariot facing the Syrians until evening, and he died at sunset — fulfilling Micaiah’s prophecy exactly.

f.g: Was held upright.

chapters.n: Jehoshaphat returned home safely to Jerusalem — a mercy, since he had nearly died in Ahab’s place.
The prophet Jehu, son of the seer who had rebuked Asa, confronts Jehoshaphat: should you help the wicked and love those who hate the Lord? God is displeased.
Yet God sees the good too: Jehoshaphat removed Asherah poles and set his heart to seek God. A rebuke and a commendation come together.

f.w: there are good things found in thee
prepared thine heart to seek God

chapters.n: Taking correction to heart, Jehoshaphat personally traveled from Beersheba in the south to Ephraim’s hills in the north, bringing people back to the Lord.

f.g: The full length of his kingdom, south to north.

chapters.n: He appointed judges in every fortified city of Judah — fitting for a king whose name means “the Lord judges.”
His charge to the judges: be careful, because you judge not for people but for the Lord, who is with you when you decide cases.

f.w: ye judge not for man, but for the LORD

chapters.n: Let reverence for God guide you, for God has no injustice, favoritism, or bribery. Judges must reflect God’s own character.

f.g: Favoritism; partiality based on status.
Accepting bribes.

chapters.n: In Jerusalem he set up a higher court of Levites, priests, and family heads to decide religious matters and difficult disputes.

f.g: Disputes or lawsuits.

chapters.n: He charged them to serve with reverence, faithfulness, and a whole heart.

f.g: With complete integrity and loyalty.

chapters.n: Whatever case comes from the towns — bloodshed, or questions of law and commandments — warn people so they don’t sin against the Lord and bring wrath on everyone.

f.g: Cases of homicide — deciding whether a killing was murder or accidental.

chapters.n: Amariah the chief priest would oversee religious matters and Zebadiah the king’s matters, with Levites as officers. Act courageously — the Lord will be with the good.

f.g: Be strong and act.

f.w: the LORD shall be with the good

chapters.n: A coalition of Moabites, Ammonites, and others (probably Meunites from Edom’s region) came to attack Jehoshaphat.

f.g: The Hebrew is unclear; many read ‘Meunites,’ a people from the region of Seir.

chapters.n: Messengers report a huge army coming from across the Dead Sea, already at En-gedi on Judah’s eastern edge — dangerously close.

f.g: The Dead Sea.
Most scholars read ‘from Edom’ (a one-letter difference in Hebrew).
An oasis on the western shore of the Dead Sea.

chapters.n: Jehoshaphat was afraid — but he responded to fear by seeking the Lord and calling a nationwide fast. Fear rightly handled drives us to God.
People came from every town in Judah to seek the Lord’s help together.
Jehoshaphat stood before the assembly in the temple, in front of the new courtyard, to lead the prayer.

f.g: Perhaps a recently renovated courtyard of the temple.

chapters.n: He begins by declaring who God is: the ruler of heaven and all nations, whose power no one can resist. Faithful prayer often starts by remembering God’s greatness.

f.w: art not thou God in heaven?

chapters.n: He recalls that God drove out the land’s former inhabitants and gave it forever to the descendants of Abraham, His friend.
Israel lived in the land and built a sanctuary for God’s name.
Jehoshaphat reminds God of Solomon’s dedicatory prayer: when disaster comes and we cry to You before this house, You will hear and save.
These invaders are the very nations God told Israel not to attack during the Exodus, because they were related to Israel through Lot and Esau.

f.w: whom thou wouldest not let Israel invade

f.g: The mountainous homeland of Edom.

chapters.n: Now they repay that kindness by trying to drive Israel out of the land God gave them.

f.g: How they repay us.

chapters.n: One of scripture’s most honest prayers: we have no power against this army and don’t know what to do — but our eyes are on You. Admitting helplessness is itself an act of faith.

f.w: neither know we what to do: but our eyes are upon thee

chapters.n: All Judah — men, women, little children — stood before the Lord, waiting for His answer.
The Spirit came upon Jahaziel, a Levite singer descended from Asaph. God answered through an unexpected person in the middle of the congregation.

f.w: came the Spirit of the LORD

chapters.n: God’s message: don’t be afraid or discouraged by this great army, for the battle is not yours, but God’s.

f.w: the battle is not yours, but God's

chapters.n: God gives specific directions: tomorrow go down to meet them as they come up the pass of Ziz at the end of the valley near the wilderness of Jeruel.

f.g: A pass climbing from the Dead Sea toward Tekoa.

chapters.n: You won’t need to fight: take your positions, stand firm, and see the Lord’s deliverance. These words echo Moses at the Red Sea.

f.w: stand ye still, and see the salvation of the LORD

chapters.n: The king bowed with his face to the ground, and everyone fell in worship before the Lord — responding to the promise before seeing it fulfilled.
Levites from the Kohathite and Korahite clans stood and praised God at the top of their voices — celebrating victory in advance.

f.g: Descendants of Korah, temple singers credited with several psalms.

chapters.n: Early the next morning Jehoshaphat told the people as they set out: believe the Lord and you’ll stand firm; believe His prophets and you’ll succeed.

f.w: Believe in the LORD your God, so shall ye be established
f.g: A Hebrew wordplay: ‘believe’ (ha’aminu) and ‘be established’ (te’amenu) share a root.

chapters.n: He put singers in front of the army to praise the beauty of holiness, singing, “Praise the LORD; for his mercy endureth for ever.” Worship led the way into battle.

f.w: for his mercy endureth for ever

chapters.n: As soon as they began singing, the Lord set ambushes against the invaders, and they were defeated.

f.g: Ambushes — perhaps caused by confusion among the enemies themselves.

chapters.n: Ammon and Moab turned on the people of Seir and destroyed them, and then turned on each other. God used their own confusion to defeat them.

f.w: every one helped to destroy another

chapters.n: When Judah reached the watchtower overlooking the desert, they saw only bodies — no one had escaped.

f.w: the watch tower in the wilderness
f.g: A lookout point overlooking the wilderness.

chapters.n: Gathering the spoil — goods, clothing, and valuables — took three full days because there was so much.

f.g: Some manuscripts read ‘garments’ instead of ‘dead bodies.’

chapters.n: On the fourth day they gathered in a valley and blessed the Lord, naming it the Valley of Berachah, “Valley of Blessing.”

f.g: Hebrew ‘blessing’.

chapters.n: Everyone returned to Jerusalem joyfully, with Jehoshaphat leading them, because the Lord had given them joy over their enemies.
They entered Jerusalem and went to the temple with lyres, harps, and trumpets — the campaign began and ended in worship.

f.g: Stringed instruments.

chapters.n: Nearby kingdoms feared God after hearing how He had fought Israel’s enemies.

f.w: the fear of God was on all the kingdoms

chapters.n: Jehoshaphat’s kingdom enjoyed peace, for God gave him rest on every side.
A summary: Jehoshaphat became king at thirty-five and ruled twenty-five years (about 872–848 BC). His mother was Azubah.
He followed in the footsteps of his father Asa and did what was right in God’s sight.
Yet the high places remained, because the people still hadn’t fully set their hearts on God. A king can lead, but each heart must choose.

f.w: the people had not prepared their hearts

chapters.n: His full history was written by the prophet Jehu son of Hanani and included in the book of the kings of Israel.
Later Jehoshaphat again allied himself with a wicked northern king — Ahaziah, Ahab’s son. He seems not to have fully learned the earlier lesson.
Together they built a fleet at Ezion-geber to sail to distant ports.

f.g: Large ocean-going ships; 1 Kings 22:48 says they were bound for Ophir.

chapters.n: The prophet Eliezer warned that because of this alliance, the Lord would destroy the project. The ships were wrecked before they could sail. Partnerships with the wicked bring loss.
Jehoshaphat died and was buried in the City of David. His son Jehoram took the throne — and Judah entered one of its darkest periods.

f.g: Also spelled Joram; not to be confused with Jehoram son of Ahab, who ruled Israel at the same time.

chapters.n: Jehoram had six brothers. The Chronicler calls Jehoshaphat “king of Israel” because he saw Judah as the true Israel, faithful to David’s house.

f.g: Chronicles often uses ‘Israel’ for God’s covenant people as a whole, including Judah.

chapters.n: Jehoshaphat gave his younger sons wealth and fortified cities but gave the throne to Jehoram, his firstborn.
Once secure in power, Jehoram murdered all his brothers and some leaders — a horrifying start that eliminated rivals and righteous influences.
Jehoram became king at thirty-two and reigned eight years (about 848–841 BC).
