He followed the wicked ways of Israel’s kings, especially Ahab’s family, because he was married to Ahab’s daughter Athaliah. One bad alliance poisoned a dynasty.

f.g: Athaliah, daughter of Ahab and probably of Jezebel.

chapters.n: Even so, God would not destroy David’s house because of His covenant to keep a “lamp” burning for David’s line. God’s faithfulness outlasts human failure.

f.g: A lamp — symbol of a continuing royal heir.

chapters.n: During his reign Edom rebelled against Judah and set up its own king.
Jehoram went out with his chariots and broke through the surrounding Edomite forces at night — but he only escaped; he did not regain control.

f.g: Surrounded him.

chapters.n: Edom stayed independent, and Libnah, a town in Judah’s lowlands, also rebelled. The Chronicler names the cause: Jehoram had forsaken the Lord.

f.g: A priestly town in the western foothills.

f.w: because he had forsaken the LORD

chapters.n: He built hill shrines throughout Judah’s mountains and led Jerusalem into spiritual adultery — unfaithfulness to God through idol worship.

f.g: In the prophets, a metaphor for idolatry — breaking the covenant ‘marriage’ with God.

chapters.n: A letter came from the prophet Elijah — the only mention of Elijah in Chronicles. Elijah may have written it before his translation, foreseeing Jehoram’s course.

f.w: a writing to him from Elijah the prophet
f.g: Elijah was taken up around this time; the letter may have been written shortly before, prophetically.

chapters.n: The charges: you followed Israel’s wicked kings, led Judah into idolatry like Ahab’s house, and murdered your brothers, who were better men than you.

f.g: To be unfaithful to God by worshipping idols.

chapters.n: God would strike his people, his family, and his possessions with a heavy blow.

f.g: A great stroke or disaster, not necessarily disease.

chapters.n: Jehoram himself would suffer a terrible, prolonged intestinal disease.
God roused the Philistines and the Arabs who lived near the Cushites against Jehoram.
They invaded Judah, plundered the palace, and carried off his wives and sons, leaving only his youngest, Jehoahaz (Ahaziah). The line of David hung by a thread.

f.g: Also called Ahaziah (the two names mean ‘the LORD has grasped’ in reversed order).

chapters.n: After all this, the Lord struck him with an incurable bowel disease, as Elijah had prophesied.
After two years of suffering he died in agony. The people gave him no memorial fire as they had for his ancestors — a sign of public disgrace.
His epitaph is one of the saddest in scripture: “he departed without being desired” — no one missed him. He was buried in Jerusalem but not in the royal tombs.

f.g: Died unmourned; no one regretted his passing.

chapters.n: Jerusalem’s people made Ahaziah, Jehoram’s youngest and only surviving son, king, since raiders had killed all the older sons.
Ahaziah reigned only one year. The text says he was forty-two, but 2 Kings says twenty-two, which fits better (his father died at forty). His mother was Athaliah, granddaughter of Omri.

f.g: Likely a copying error; 2 Kings 8:26 and some ancient versions read 22.
Granddaughter — Omri was Ahab’s father.

chapters.n: Ahaziah also followed Ahab’s family ways, because his mother counseled him to do evil. A parent’s influence can lead a child toward God or away.

f.w: his mother was his counsellor to do wickedly

chapters.n: After his father’s death, Ahab’s relatives became his advisers — and led him to ruin.
Following their advice, Ahaziah joined Israel’s King Jehoram (Joram), Ahab’s son, in battle against Hazael of Syria at Ramoth-gilead, where Joram was wounded.
Joram went to Jezreel to recover, and Ahaziah (here called Azariah) went to visit him. This visit put him in the path of judgment.

f.g: A copying variant of Ahaziah.
Short for Ramoth-gilead.

chapters.n: God used this visit to bring about Ahaziah’s downfall: he went out with Joram to meet Jehu, whom the Lord had anointed to wipe out Ahab’s house.
While executing judgment on Ahab’s house, Jehu also killed Judah’s princes and Ahaziah’s nephews who were with him.

f.w: the sons of the brethren of Ahaziah

chapters.n: Ahaziah was found hiding, brought to Jehu, and killed. He received a burial only out of respect for his grandfather Jehoshaphat, who sought the Lord wholeheartedly. No one in his family could hold the kingdom.

f.w: who sought the LORD with all his heart

chapters.n: When Athaliah learned her son was dead, she seized power and set out to murder the entire royal family of Judah — even her own grandchildren. David’s line came close to ending.

f.g: All the royal descendants who could claim the throne.

chapters.n: But Jehoshabeath, Ahaziah’s sister and wife of the priest Jehoiada, rescued the infant Joash and hid him with his nurse in a bedroom. One courageous woman preserved the line through which the Messiah would come.

f.g: Called Jehosheba in 2 Kings 11:2.

chapters.n: Joash was hidden in God’s temple for six years while Athaliah ruled. God’s house sheltered the hope of His promise.

f.w: hid in the house of God six years

chapters.n: In the seventh year, Jehoiada the priest took courage and made a covenant with five army commanders to restore the rightful king.

f.g: Took courage; acted boldly.

chapters.n: These commanders secretly gathered Levites and family leaders from throughout Judah to Jerusalem.
In the temple, the assembly made a covenant with the young king. Jehoiada declared: the king’s son shall reign, as God promised regarding David’s descendants.

f.w: as the LORD hath said of the sons of David

chapters.n: Jehoiada’s plan used the Sabbath shift change: a third of the incoming priests and Levites would guard the doors.

f.g: Gatekeepers.

chapters.n: Another third would be at the palace and another at the Foundation Gate, with the people gathered in the temple courts.

f.g: Probably a temple gate; 2 Kings 11:6 calls it the gate Sur.

chapters.n: Only priests and ministering Levites, who were consecrated, could enter the temple building; everyone else would guard outside. Even in a crisis, holy space was respected.

f.w: keep the watch of the LORD
f.g: Observe the Lord’s requirements; keep their assigned posts.

chapters.n: Armed Levites were to surround the king and kill anyone who forced their way into the temple, staying with him at all times.
Everyone followed Jehoiada’s orders. He kept both the incoming and outgoing shifts on duty, doubling the guard.

f.g: Did not release the divisions going off duty.

chapters.n: Jehoiada armed the commanders with King David’s own spears and shields kept in the temple — a fitting symbol for restoring David’s heir.

f.g: Small round shields.

chapters.n: Armed guards formed a protective line across the temple court, around the altar and the king.
They brought out the seven-year-old prince, crowned him, gave him “the testimony” (a copy of God’s law), and anointed him. The people shouted, “Long live the king!”

f.g: Likely the covenant law, which the king was to keep and study.
Hebrew ‘Let the king live!’

chapters.n: Athaliah heard the noise of people running and cheering, and came into the temple.
She saw the boy king standing by his pillar at the entrance, surrounded by officers, trumpeters, and rejoicing crowds. She tore her clothes and screamed “Treason!” — though she was the real usurper.

f.g: The king’s customary place by a temple pillar.
Hebrew qesher — conspiracy.

chapters.n: Jehoiada ordered the commanders to take her out between the ranks of soldiers and kill anyone who followed her — but not to kill her in the Lord’s house.

f.w: Have her forth of the ranges
f.g: Bring her out between the rows of guards.

chapters.n: They seized her and executed her at the Horse Gate entrance to the palace.
Jehoiada renewed the covenant: he, the people, and the king pledged to be the Lord’s people. Renewing covenants restores identity.

f.w: that they should be the LORD's people

chapters.n: The people tore down Baal’s temple, smashed its altars and images, and killed Mattan, Baal’s priest. Athaliah’s imported religion was removed.

f.g: A temple for Baal built in Jerusalem, probably under Athaliah.

chapters.n: Jehoiada restored temple service under the priests and Levites as David had organized it, with burnt offerings according to Moses’ law and joyful singing as David ordained.

f.w: as it is written in the law of Moses
as it was ordained by David

chapters.n: He stationed gatekeepers so no one ritually unclean could enter the temple — protecting its holiness.

f.w: that none which was unclean in any thing should enter in

chapters.n: With leaders and people, Jehoiada escorted the king from the temple through the Upper Gate into the palace and seated him on the throne.

f.g: The upper gate, connecting the temple and palace areas.

chapters.n: The people rejoiced and the city was at peace after Athaliah’s death. David’s line was restored.
Joash became king at seven and reigned forty years (about 835–796 BC). His mother Zibiah was from Beersheba.

f.g: Also spelled Jehoash.

chapters.n: Joash did right as long as Jehoiada the priest lived. His faithfulness depended on his mentor — a warning about borrowed faith.

f.w: all the days of Jehoiada the priest

chapters.n: Jehoiada arranged two marriages for Joash, and he had children — rebuilding the nearly extinct royal line of David.
Joash, who had grown up hidden in the temple, set his heart on repairing it.

f.g: Resolved; set his heart.

chapters.n: He told the priests and Levites to collect money yearly from all Israel for the repairs and to do it quickly — but the Levites delayed.

f.g: Did not act quickly.

chapters.n: Joash confronted Jehoiada: why haven’t you required the Levites to collect the tax Moses commanded for the tabernacle?

f.g: The half-shekel offering for the sanctuary.
The tent of the testimony, which housed the covenant tablets.

chapters.n: The repairs were urgent because Athaliah’s sons had broken into the temple and used its holy things to worship the Baals.

f.g: The only time Chronicles uses such a direct label for a person.
Broken into and damaged.

chapters.n: So the king had a chest made and placed outside the temple gate — a public collection box.
A proclamation went out throughout Judah to bring the offering Moses had required in the wilderness.
Leaders and people gave joyfully, filling the chest until the need was met. Willing, joyful giving echoes the offerings for the tabernacle and David’s temple.
When the chest filled, the king’s secretary and the high priest’s officer emptied it and returned it. They collected large amounts this way, with careful accountability.

f.g: The royal secretary.

chapters.n: The king and Jehoiada paid stonemasons, carpenters, and ironworkers to restore the temple.

f.g: Stoneworkers.

chapters.n: The workers labored faithfully until the temple was restored to its original condition and strengthened.

f.g: To its proper condition; according to its design.

chapters.n: Leftover money was used to make gold and silver vessels for temple worship, and regular burnt offerings continued throughout Jehoiada’s lifetime.

f.g: Utensils for temple service.

chapters.n: Jehoiada lived to the great age of 130 — a sign in scripture of God’s favor on a righteous life.
Jehoiada was honored with burial among the kings — a priest buried as royalty — because of the good he did for God, His house, and Israel.
After Jehoiada’s death, Judah’s officials came, bowed to Joash with flattery, and he listened to them. Without his mentor, he followed new voices.

f.g: Bowed down in honor — perhaps flattery to win the king’s favor.

chapters.n: They abandoned the temple and worshipped Asherah poles and idols, and God’s anger came on Judah and Jerusalem. The temple Joash repaired was now forsaken.

f.g: Asherah poles.

chapters.n: Still, God sent prophets to bring them back. The prophets warned them, but they refused to listen. God’s patience is shown in repeated warnings.
The Spirit came upon Zechariah, Jehoiada’s son, who stood above the people and asked: why break God’s commandments, so you can’t prosper? Because you left the Lord, He has left you.

f.w: because ye have forsaken the LORD, he hath also forsaken you

chapters.n: They plotted against him and, at the king’s command, stoned him in the temple courtyard. Jesus later referred to this murder as among the last martyrdoms recorded in the Hebrew Bible.
Joash forgot the kindness of Jehoiada, who had saved his life and crown, and killed his son. Zechariah’s dying words: “May the Lord see and avenge.”

f.w: The LORD look upon it, and require it
f.g: May God see this and call the guilty to account.

chapters.n: Within a year, a Syrian army invaded Judah and Jerusalem, killed the officials who had led the people astray, and sent the plunder to Damascus.

f.g: The same leaders who had turned Joash to idolatry (v.17).

chapters.n: Though the Syrian force was small, God gave Judah’s huge army into their hands because Judah had forsaken Him. They carried out judgment on Joash.
Wounded and sick, Joash was murdered in his bed by his own officials as revenge for killing Jehoiada’s son. He was buried in Jerusalem but not in the royal tombs where Jehoiada lay.

f.g: The plural may emphasize the crime, or include other sons.

chapters.n: The conspirators were Zabad and Jehozabad, sons of Ammonite and Moabite mothers. The Chronicler notes their foreign mothers, perhaps echoing the idolatry Joash embraced.

f.g: Called Jozachar in 2 Kings 12:21.

chapters.n: Further details about Joash’s sons, the prophecies against him, and the temple repairs were in the commentary on the book of the kings. His son Amaziah succeeded him.

f.w: the story of the book of the kings
f.g: Hebrew midrash — an explanatory account or commentary.
Probably ‘oracles’ — prophetic messages against him.

chapters.n: Amaziah became king at twenty-five and reigned twenty-nine years (about 796–767 BC). His mother was Jehoaddan of Jerusalem.
He did what was right — but not wholeheartedly. This one phrase summarizes his whole reign: outward obedience with a divided heart.
Once firmly in power, he executed the officials who had murdered his father Joash.
But he spared their children, obeying Moses’ law that each person dies for his own sin. Justice punishes the guilty, not the innocent.

f.w: every man shall die for his own sin

chapters.n: Amaziah organized Judah and Benjamin’s army by families and counted 300,000 men twenty and older.

f.w: from twenty years old and above

chapters.n: He also hired 100,000 soldiers from northern Israel for 100 talents of silver (about 3.75 tons).
A man of God warned him not to use Israel’s troops, for the Lord was not with Ephraim (the northern kingdom), which had turned to idols.

f.g: The leading tribe of the north, often a name for the whole northern kingdom.

chapters.n: Even if you fight bravely, God will make you fall, because God alone has power to help or to overthrow.

f.w: God hath power to help, and to cast down

chapters.n: Amaziah worried about losing his money. The prophet’s answer is timeless: “The LORD is able to give thee much more than this.” Obedience may cost, but God can repay.

f.w: The LORD is able to give thee much more than this

chapters.n: Amaziah sent the hired troops home. They left furious at Judah, insulted at being dismissed.
Strengthened, Amaziah led his army to the Valley of Salt, south of the Dead Sea, and killed 10,000 Edomites.

f.g: The Edomites.

chapters.n: Judah also captured 10,000 more and executed them by throwing them from a cliff — a brutal act the text reports without approval.

f.g: Possibly Sela (‘the Rock’), an Edomite stronghold, perhaps near later Petra.

chapters.n: Meanwhile, the dismissed Israelite soldiers raided Judah’s towns from Samaria to Beth-horon, killing 3,000 and taking much plunder.
Shockingly, after defeating Edom, Amaziah brought back Edom’s gods and worshipped them — gods that had just failed to protect their own people.

f.w: set them up to be his gods

chapters.n: God sent a prophet with a pointed question: why seek gods that couldn’t even save their own people from you?

f.w: which could not deliver their own people

chapters.n: Amaziah cut him off: “Have we made you the king’s adviser? Stop — or you’ll be struck down.” The prophet stopped, but warned that God had determined to destroy him for refusing counsel.

f.w: Art thou made of the king's counsel?
f.g: Who appointed you royal adviser?
Stop; be quiet.

f.w: hast not hearkened unto my counsel

chapters.n: Proud from his victory, Amaziah challenged Joash, king of Israel, to battle: “Let us face each other.”

f.w: let us see one another in the face
f.g: An idiom for meeting in battle.

chapters.n: Joash answered with a parable: a thistle asked a cedar for its daughter in marriage, and a wild beast trampled the thistle. Amaziah was the thistle, overreaching.

f.w: The thistle that was in Lebanon

chapters.n: Joash warned him: your victory over Edom has made you arrogant. Stay home — why provoke trouble that will ruin you and Judah?
Amaziah wouldn’t listen. God allowed his stubbornness to bring defeat, because Judah had sought Edom’s gods.
Joash marched against him, and the two kings met at Beth-shemesh in Judah.

f.g: A town on Judah’s western border.

chapters.n: Judah was routed, and every man fled home.
Joash captured Amaziah, brought him to Jerusalem, and tore down 400 cubits (about 600 feet) of the city wall — humiliating Judah.

f.w: the gate of Ephraim to the corner gate
f.g: A stretch of the northern wall facing Israel.

chapters.n: He seized gold, silver, and vessels from the temple (kept by Obed-edom’s family), the palace treasures, and hostages, and returned to Samaria.

f.g: A family of Levite gatekeepers responsible for temple storehouses.

chapters.n: Amaziah lived fifteen years after Joash of Israel died.
The rest of Amaziah’s history was in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel.
From the time he turned from the Lord, a conspiracy formed against him. He fled to Lachish, but was pursued and killed there.
His body was brought back on horses and buried with his ancestors in the City of David.

f.g: Jerusalem; 2 Kings 14:20 reads ‘city of David.’

chapters.n: The people of Judah made sixteen-year-old Uzziah king after his father Amaziah.

f.g: Also called Azariah in Kings; both names mean roughly ‘the LORD is my strength/help.’

chapters.n: He rebuilt Eloth (Elath), the Red Sea port, and returned it to Judah, reopening trade routes.

f.g: Elath, on the Gulf of Aqaba.

chapters.n: Uzziah reigned fifty-two years (about 792–740 BC, including years co-reigning) — one of Judah’s longest reigns. His mother was Jecoliah of Jerusalem.
He did right in the Lord’s sight, as his father had in his better years.
He sought God during the lifetime of Zechariah, a teacher who understood the visions (or ‘fear’) of God. As long as he sought the Lord, God made him prosper — the key verse of his life.

f.g: A spiritual adviser otherwise unknown; not the later prophet.

f.w: as long as he sought the LORD, God made him to prosper

chapters.n: He fought the Philistines, broke down the walls of Gath, Jabneh, and Ashdod, and built towns in Philistine territory.

f.g: Later Jamnia (Yavneh), near the coast.
One of the five main Philistine cities.

chapters.n: God helped him against the Philistines, the Arabs of Gur-baal, and the Meunites.

f.g: Meunites, a people of the Arabian or Edomite region.

chapters.n: The Ammonites paid him tribute, and his fame reached Egypt’s border because he became very powerful.
Uzziah built and fortified towers in Jerusalem at the Corner Gate, the Valley Gate, and the Angle — partly repairing damage from his father’s defeat.

f.g: The angle or bend in the wall.

chapters.n: He built towers and dug wells in the wilderness for his herds, and employed farmers and vinedressers, for he loved the soil. A king who cared for agriculture strengthened his people’s livelihood.

f.g: Farming; working the soil.
Here probably meaning fertile land or orchards, not necessarily Mount Carmel.

chapters.n: He had a well-organized army, mustered by divisions under the scribe Jeiel and the official Maaseiah, supervised by Hananiah.

f.g: In organized divisions.

chapters.n: The army had 2,600 family heads as officers.
Under them were 307,500 trained soldiers ready to defend the king.
Uzziah equipped his whole army with shields, spears, helmets, armor, bows, and slingstones — unusual, since soldiers often had to supply their own gear.

f.g: Coats of mail; body armor.

chapters.n: He built inventive devices on Jerusalem’s towers to shoot arrows and hurl large stones. His fame spread, for he was marvelously helped — until he became strong.

f.g: Machines of war — perhaps defensive frameworks or early catapults.
A warning phrase: help from God until strength led to pride.

chapters.n: But strength led to pride. Uzziah entered the temple to burn incense on the incense altar — a sacred duty given only to priests.

f.w: his heart was lifted up to his destruction

chapters.n: Azariah the high priest followed him in with eighty courageous priests to stop him.

f.g: Brave men — it took courage to confront the king.

chapters.n: They confronted the king: burning incense isn’t your right, Uzziah, but belongs to Aaron’s consecrated descendants. Leave the sanctuary — you have sinned. Priesthood authority cannot be taken, only given by God.

f.g: It does not belong to you.

chapters.n: Uzziah, censer in hand, raged at the priests — and right then leprosy broke out on his forehead beside the incense altar.

f.g: A term for various serious skin diseases that made one ritually unclean.

chapters.n: Seeing the leprosy on his forehead, the priests hurried him out — and he hurried to leave, for the Lord had struck him.

f.g: Hurried him out.

chapters.n: Uzziah remained leprous until death, living in isolation and barred from the temple. His son Jotham governed in his place. The king who reached for priestly power lost even ordinary access to God’s house.

f.g: A separate house — quarantine.

chapters.n: Isaiah the prophet wrote the rest of Uzziah’s history. Isaiah’s great vision of the Lord came “in the year that king Uzziah died.”

f.w: Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz

chapters.n: Uzziah was buried in a field next to the royal tombs, not in them, because he was a leper. Jotham became king.
Jotham became king at twenty-five and reigned sixteen years (about 750–735 BC, partly as regent for his leprous father). His mother Jerushah was a daughter of Zadok, perhaps from the priestly family.

f.g: Name means ‘the LORD is perfect.’

chapters.n: Jotham did right like his father — but, unlike Uzziah, he did not intrude into the temple. Sadly, the people still acted corruptly; a good king could not force good hearts.

f.w: he entered not into the temple of the LORD
f.g: He did not repeat Uzziah’s sin of usurping the priests’ role.

chapters.n: He built the Upper Gate of the temple and did extensive work on the wall of Ophel, the hill between the temple and the City of David.

f.g: The fortified ridge just south of the temple mount.

chapters.n: He built towns in Judah’s hill country and forts and towers in the wooded areas to protect the land.

f.g: Fortresses.

chapters.n: Jotham defeated the Ammonites, who paid him heavy tribute — 100 talents of silver and 10,000 measures each of wheat and barley — for three years.

f.g: Hebrew kor — a large dry measure, about 6 bushels.

chapters.n: Jotham became strong because he ordered his life before the Lord his God. Steady, deliberate faithfulness brings strength.

f.w: he prepared his ways before the LORD
f.g: He established or directed his conduct according to God’s will.

chapters.n: His wars and other deeds were recorded in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah.
The Chronicler repeats his age and length of reign, perhaps to close his story neatly.
Jotham died and was buried in the City of David. His son Ahaz, one of Judah’s worst kings, succeeded him.
Ahaz became king at twenty and reigned sixteen years (about 735–715 BC). Unlike his ancestor David, he did not do what was right in God’s sight.

f.g: The same king to whom Isaiah gave the sign of Immanuel.

chapters.n: He followed the northern kings’ idolatry and even made cast-metal idols of the Baals.

f.g: Idols made of cast metal.

chapters.n: He burned incense in the Valley of Hinnom and sacrificed his own children in fire — the horrifying practices of the Canaanites God had driven out. This valley later gave its name to “Gehenna,” a symbol of hell.

f.w: the valley of the son of Hinnom
f.g: A valley south of Jerusalem; its Greek name Gehenna became a term for the place of punishment.

f.w: burnt his children in the fire

chapters.n: He offered sacrifices at high places, on hills, and under every leafy tree — sites of pagan fertility worship.
So God handed him over to Syria, which took many captives to Damascus, and to Israel, which inflicted heavy losses.

f.g: Rezin, who allied with Israel against Judah.

chapters.n: Pekah, king of Israel, killed 120,000 of Judah’s soldiers in one day, because they had forsaken the Lord.
An Ephraimite warrior named Zichri killed the king’s son and two top officials, decapitating Judah’s leadership.

f.g: The palace administrator.

chapters.n: Israel took 200,000 captives from Judah — their own relatives — along with much plunder, to Samaria.

f.g: Fellow Israelites — kinsmen.

chapters.n: A prophet named Oded met the returning army and warned: God let you defeat Judah because He was angry with them — but you slaughtered them with a rage that reaches heaven.

f.g: A northern prophet, otherwise unknown; not the same Oded of 2 Chronicles 15.

f.w: a rage that reacheth up unto heaven

chapters.n: Now you plan to enslave your own relatives — but aren’t you guilty of sins against the Lord too?

f.g: Subjugate; enslave.

chapters.n: So listen: send the captives home, for God’s fierce anger is on you.
Four leaders of Ephraim stood up to confront the returning soldiers. Righteous leaders in a wicked kingdom chose to do right.
They said: you shall not bring the captives here — we’re guilty enough already, and this would add to our sin.

f.g: Guilt; unfaithfulness.

chapters.n: The soldiers gave up the captives and plunder before the leaders and assembly.

The named leaders clothed the naked captives, gave them sandals, food, drink, and soothing oil, put the weak on donkeys, and returned them to their families at Jericho. Many see this as the background of Jesus’ parable of the Good Samaritan.

f.g: Applied oil to their wounds or skin — a sign of care and refreshment.

f.w: Jericho, the city of palm trees

chapters.n: Meanwhile Ahaz asked the king of Assyria for help instead of turning to God — despite Isaiah urging him to trust the Lord.
Edom had again invaded Judah and carried off captives.
The Philistines seized many towns in Judah’s western foothills and the Negev and settled in them — losses of territory Uzziah had won.

f.g: The Shephelah — the western foothills.

chapters.n: God humbled Judah because of Ahaz, who let Judah run wild (“made Judah naked”) and sinned grievously. He is called “king of Israel” as ruler of God’s covenant people.

f.g: He let Judah throw off restraint, or left Judah defenseless.

chapters.n: Tiglath-pileser of Assyria came — but brought trouble rather than help. Trusting worldly powers instead of God backfires.

f.g: Tiglath-pileser III, king of Assyria (about 745–727 BC).

chapters.n: Ahaz stripped the temple, palace, and officials’ treasures to pay Assyria, but it did not help him.
In his distress he sinned even more. The Chronicler adds sharply: “this is that king Ahaz” — this was the kind of man he was.

f.w: in the time of his distress

chapters.n: He sacrificed to Damascus’s gods, reasoning that since they helped Syria, they would help him. Instead they ruined him and all Israel.
He cut up the temple vessels, shut the temple doors, and set up altars on every street corner in Jerusalem — formally ending the worship of the Lord at His house.

f.w: shut up the doors of the house of the LORD

chapters.n: In every town he built shrines for other gods, provoking the God of his fathers.

f.g: Each and every city.

chapters.n: His history was written in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel.
Ahaz was buried in Jerusalem but not in the royal tombs — a mark of dishonor. His son Hezekiah, one of Judah’s greatest kings, succeeded him.

f.g: Name means ‘the LORD strengthens.’

chapters.n: Hezekiah became king at twenty-five and reigned twenty-nine years (about 715–686 BC). His mother was Abijah, daughter of Zechariah.
He did right in God’s sight just as David had — high praise reserved for very few kings.

f.w: according to all that David his father had done

chapters.n: In the very first month of his reign, Hezekiah reopened and repaired the temple doors his father had shut. He made restoring worship his first priority.
He gathered the priests and Levites in the square on the east side of the temple.

f.g: An open square east of the temple.

chapters.n: He commanded the Levites to purify themselves and the temple and carry out the defilement — the idols and debris from Ahaz’s reign. Personal purity comes before cleansing God’s house.

f.g: Ritually unclean things — idols and their equipment.

chapters.n: Hezekiah openly confesses: our fathers sinned, forsook God, and turned their backs on His house. Honest confession begins renewal.
They had shut the doors, put out the lamps, and stopped incense and burnt offerings — silencing the house of God.

f.g: The lampstand was to burn continually before the Lord.

chapters.n: So God’s anger came on Judah, making it a horror and a thing people hissed at, as everyone could see.

f.g: A sound of contempt and shock.

chapters.n: Our fathers died in battle, and our families are in captivity because of this.
Hezekiah resolves to make a covenant with the Lord so His fierce anger may turn away. Renewal comes through covenant.
He addresses the Levites tenderly as “my sons”: don’t be negligent now — God chose you to stand before Him and serve.

f.g: Don’t be careless or slack.

chapters.n: Levites from all three main clans — Kohath, Merari, and Gershon — responded, two leaders from each.
Also from the clan of Elizaphan and from the singing family of Asaph.

f.g: A leading Kohathite family.

chapters.n: And from the singer families of Heman and Jeduthun. Fourteen leaders in all stepped up.
They gathered their brothers, purified themselves, and began cleansing the temple as the king commanded, following the Lord’s word.

f.w: by the words of the LORD
f.g: According to the law God had given.

chapters.n: The priests cleaned the inner rooms and brought everything unclean out to the courtyard; the Levites carried it out to the Kidron Valley.
The work began on the first day of the first month; in eight days they reached the porch, and in eight more they finished — sixteen days in all.

f.w: the first day of the first month
f.g: The month of Nisan, when Passover would normally be held on the 14th.

chapters.n: They reported to Hezekiah that the whole temple, the altar, the bread table, and their utensils were cleansed.
They had also restored and purified the vessels Ahaz had discarded, and set them before the altar.

f.g: Discarded or removed.

chapters.n: Early the next morning Hezekiah gathered the city’s leaders and went up to the temple.

f.g: A sign of eagerness.

chapters.n: They brought seven each of bulls, rams, lambs, and goats as a sin offering for the kingdom, the sanctuary, and Judah. Seven signals completeness.
Priests slaughtered the animals and sprinkled their blood on the altar.
The goats for the sin offering were brought before the king and assembly, who laid hands on them — symbolically transferring their sins to the offering.

f.w: they laid their hands upon them

chapters.n: The priests made atonement with the goats’ blood for “all Israel” — including the northern tribes. Hezekiah wanted to reunite God’s whole people. These sacrifices pointed to Christ’s atoning blood.

f.w: to make an atonement for all Israel

f.g: Hebrew ḥatta’ — purification from sin.

chapters.n: He stationed Levites with cymbals, lyres, and harps, as commanded by David and the prophets Gad and Nathan — for the music too came by revelation.

f.w: for so was the commandment of the LORD by his prophets

chapters.n: The Levites stood with David’s instruments and the priests with trumpets.
As the burnt offering began, so did the “song of the LORD,” with trumpets and instruments. Sacrifice and song went together.

f.g: Sacred music for worship.

chapters.n: The whole assembly worshipped while singers sang and trumpets sounded until the offering was finished.
Afterward the king and all present bowed and worshipped.
Hezekiah had the Levites sing praises with the words of David and Asaph — psalms we still have — and they sang joyfully and bowed in worship.

f.g: Asaph is credited with Psalms 50 and 73–83.

chapters.n: Hezekiah invited the people, now consecrated, to bring sacrifices and thank offerings. Many, with willing hearts, brought burnt offerings too.

f.g: Literally ‘filled your hand’ — dedicated yourselves.
Willing; generous.

chapters.n: The people brought 70 bulls, 100 rams, and 200 lambs as burnt offerings.
Other consecrated offerings totaled 600 cattle and 3,000 sheep.
There weren’t enough purified priests to skin all the offerings, so Levites helped, because the Levites had been more diligent in purifying themselves than the priests.

f.g: Skin the animals.

chapters.n: With abundant offerings, fat of peace offerings, and drink offerings, temple worship was restored in proper order.

f.g: Re-established; organized.

chapters.n: Hezekiah and the people rejoiced at how God had prepared them, for it all happened so quickly. Rapid renewal was itself God’s gift.
Hezekiah invited all Israel and Judah — even the northern tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh — to Jerusalem to keep the Passover. He reached across the old division to reunite God’s people in worship.

f.g: Leading northern tribes, representing the remnant of the northern kingdom after Assyria’s conquest.

chapters.n: The king, officials, and assembly decided to hold Passover in the second month instead of the first.

f.g: The law allowed a second-month Passover for those unable to keep it on time.

chapters.n: They couldn’t hold it at the normal time because not enough priests had been purified and the people hadn’t yet gathered.

f.w: the priests had not sanctified themselves sufficiently

chapters.n: The plan pleased the king and the whole assembly.
They proclaimed it from Beersheba to Dan — the whole land — because Passover hadn’t been kept as prescribed for a long time.

f.g: From the far south to the far north — all Israel.

chapters.n: Couriers carried letters urging: Israel, return to the Lord, and He will return to you — the remnant who escaped Assyria. Turning to God brings God turning to us.

f.g: Couriers; runners.

chapters.n: Don’t be like your fathers and brothers who were unfaithful and were given over to ruin, as you can see for yourselves.
Don’t be stubborn like your ancestors; yield to the Lord, come to His sanctuary, and serve Him, so His anger turns away.

f.g: Stubborn, like an ox refusing the yoke.
Literally ‘give the hand to the LORD’ — pledge yourselves.

chapters.n: If you return, your exiled relatives will find mercy from their captors and come home, for the Lord is gracious and merciful and will not turn His face away. A promise of gathering for those who return.

f.w: the LORD your God is gracious and merciful

chapters.n: The couriers went town to town through Ephraim, Manasseh, and Zebulun, but most people laughed at and mocked them.
Still, some from Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun humbled themselves and came to Jerusalem. Humility opens the way back.

f.g: Some; various people.

chapters.n: In Judah, God’s hand gave the people unity of heart to obey the king and officials, who followed the Lord’s word.
A huge crowd gathered in Jerusalem for the Feast of Unleavened Bread in the second month.

f.g: The seven-day festival following Passover.

chapters.n: First they removed the pagan altars and incense altars Ahaz had set up all over Jerusalem and threw them into the Kidron Valley.

f.w: the altars that were in Jerusalem

chapters.n: They slaughtered the Passover lambs on the fourteenth of the second month. Priests and Levites, ashamed of their lack of readiness, purified themselves and brought burnt offerings. The people’s zeal shamed the clergy into action.
Priests and Levites took their places according to Moses’ law; the priests sprinkled the blood that the Levites handed to them.
Many in the crowd were not ritually clean, so the Levites slaughtered the Passover lambs for them to keep the offering holy.
Many northerners ate the Passover without proper purification — contrary to the law. But Hezekiah prayed: “May the good LORD pardon everyone…”

f.w: The good LORD pardon every one

chapters.n: “…who sets his heart to seek God, even if not purified by the sanctuary’s rules.” Hezekiah understood God values a sincere heart above ritual technicalities.

f.w: That prepareth his heart to seek God

chapters.n: The Lord heard Hezekiah and healed the people. God honored a prayer of mercy for sincere seekers.
Israel kept the seven-day feast with great joy, and the priests and Levites praised the Lord daily with loud instruments.

f.g: Literally ‘instruments of strength’ — powerful music.

chapters.n: Hezekiah encouraged the Levites who taught the good knowledge of the Lord. All week the people ate, offered peace offerings, and gave thanks (or confessed) to God.

f.g: Spoke encouragingly; literally ‘spoke to the heart.’
Giving thanks or confessing — the Hebrew can mean both.

chapters.n: The whole assembly decided to celebrate seven more days, and did so joyfully. Joy in worship was so great they didn’t want it to end.
Hezekiah gave 1,000 bulls and 7,000 sheep, and the officials gave 1,000 bulls and 10,000 sheep. Many more priests purified themselves.

f.g: Contributed as offerings for the people’s feasting.

chapters.n: Everyone rejoiced — Judah, priests and Levites, those from Israel, and foreigners living among them. A celebration of unity.

f.g: Resident foreigners who had joined Israel’s worship.

chapters.n: Jerusalem hadn’t seen such joy since the days of Solomon — the temple’s dedication.
The priests and Levites blessed the people, and their prayer reached God’s holy dwelling in heaven. The temple on earth was linked to God’s home above.

f.w: his holy dwelling place, even unto heaven

chapters.n: Inspired by the Passover, the worshippers went out and destroyed idols, Asherah poles, high places, and altars across Judah, Benjamin, and even Ephraim and Manasseh. Worship led to action. Then they returned home.

f.g: Asherah poles.

chapters.n: Hezekiah reorganized the priests and Levites into their rotating divisions, each with his duties — sacrifice, ministry, thanksgiving, and praise at the gates of the Lord’s house.

f.g: The temple, called by the old tabernacle term.

chapters.n: The king contributed from his own wealth for the daily, Sabbath, new moon, and festival burnt offerings, as the law required. Leaders give first.

f.w: as it is written in the law of the LORD

chapters.n: He commanded Jerusalem’s residents to give the priests’ and Levites’ portion, so these servants could devote themselves fully to God’s law.

f.w: that they might be encouraged in the law
f.g: That they could be devoted (literally ‘strong’) in the law, free from other labor.

chapters.n: As soon as the order went out, Israel generously brought firstfruits of grain, wine, oil, honey, and produce, and abundant tithes of everything.

f.g: Grain.

chapters.n: Those living in Judah’s towns brought tithes of cattle and sheep and holy gifts, piling them up in heaps.

f.g: In piles — so much it had to be stacked.

chapters.n: They began piling up offerings in the third month (harvest of grain) and finished in the seventh (harvest of fruit and grapes).

f.g: Around the Feast of Weeks and wheat harvest.
Around the Feast of Tabernacles and fruit harvest.

chapters.n: When Hezekiah and the officials saw the heaps, they praised the Lord and blessed His people.
Hezekiah asked the priests and Levites about the heaps.
Azariah the chief priest explained: since the offerings began, we’ve had plenty to eat with lots left over, because the Lord has blessed His people. A fulfillment of God’s promise for tithing.

f.w: we have had enough to eat, and have left plenty

chapters.n: Hezekiah ordered storerooms prepared in the temple.

f.g: Storerooms.

chapters.n: The offerings, tithes, and dedicated gifts were brought in faithfully, managed by the Levite Cononiah and his brother Shimei.

f.g: With honesty and integrity.

chapters.n: Ten overseers worked under them, appointed by the king and the chief priest. Careful organization ensured sacred funds were handled well.
Kore, gatekeeper of the East Gate, was in charge of freewill offerings and distributing the most holy portions.

f.g: Offerings.
Offerings only priests could eat.

chapters.n: Assistants in the priests’ towns faithfully distributed portions to their fellow priests by divisions, to old and young alike.

f.g: In their position of trust.

f.w: the great as to the small
f.g: Older and younger, or higher and lower rank.

chapters.n: They also gave daily portions to males three years and older registered in the genealogies who entered the temple for service.

f.g: Official family registers that determined priestly eligibility.

chapters.n: Distribution followed the genealogies of priests by families and Levites twenty and older by their duties.
Their whole families — wives, sons, daughters, little ones — were included, because they had consecrated themselves faithfully.

f.g: Kept themselves dedicated in their trusted service.

chapters.n: Men were also appointed in every priestly town and its pasturelands to distribute portions to all priests and registered Levites.

f.g: Pasturelands around the towns.
Specifically designated by name.

chapters.n: Hezekiah did this throughout Judah, doing what was good, right, and faithful before the Lord.
In everything he undertook for God’s house, law, and commandments, he sought God wholeheartedly — and he prospered. Wholehearted effort is the Chronicler’s formula for blessing.

f.w: he did it with all his heart, and prospered

chapters.n: After Hezekiah’s faithful reforms, Sennacherib of Assyria invaded Judah (701 BC) and besieged its fortified cities. Faithfulness doesn’t exempt us from trials, but it prepares us for them.

f.g: Ruled Assyria about 705–681 BC; his own annals boast of shutting Hezekiah up in Jerusalem ‘like a bird in a cage.’

chapters.n: Hezekiah saw that Sennacherib intended to attack Jerusalem itself.
With his officials and warriors, he decided to block the springs outside the city, and they supported him.

f.g: Cover or divert the springs so the enemy would lack water.

chapters.n: Many people helped seal the springs and the stream, asking, “Why should Assyria’s kings find plenty of water?”

f.w: the brook that ran through the midst of the land
f.g: Probably the stream flowing from the Gihon spring in the Kidron Valley.

chapters.n: Hezekiah rebuilt the broken wall, raised towers, built a second outer wall, reinforced the Millo, and made many weapons. Faith and preparation work together.

f.g: Archaeologists have found a thick wall in Jerusalem dated to Hezekiah’s time, the ‘Broad Wall.’
Terraced fortifications in the City of David.
Spears or javelins.

chapters.n: He appointed commanders and gathered the people in the square at the city gate to encourage them.

f.g: Spoke encouragingly — literally ‘to their heart.’

chapters.n: Be strong and courageous; don’t fear Assyria’s king or his army, for there are more with us than with him — words echoing Elisha’s vision of heavenly armies.

f.w: there be more with us than with him

chapters.n: “With him is an arm of flesh; but with us is the LORD our God.” Human power versus divine help — the people were steadied by these words.

f.g: Merely human strength.
Relied on; took confidence from.

chapters.n: While Sennacherib besieged Lachish with his main army, he sent officials to Jerusalem with a message for Hezekiah and the people.

f.g: Sennacherib’s siege of Lachish is pictured in stone reliefs from his palace at Nineveh, now in the British Museum.

chapters.n: Sennacherib’s message: “What are you trusting in, to stay under siege in Jerusalem?” He tried to undermine their faith.
Isn’t Hezekiah deceiving you into dying of hunger and thirst by claiming the Lord will save you?

f.g: Mislead; incite.

chapters.n: He twisted Hezekiah’s reforms into an insult: hasn’t Hezekiah removed the Lord’s own shrines and told you to worship at only one altar? The Assyrians misunderstood that this was obedience, not disrespect.
Don’t you know what my ancestors and I have done to other nations? Their gods couldn’t save them.
Which god of any nation we destroyed could rescue his people? How then could yours?

f.g: Completely devoted to destruction.

chapters.n: Don’t let Hezekiah deceive you. No god has stopped us — how much less will your God! His mistake was to treat the living God like a lifeless idol.

f.w: how much less shall your God deliver you

chapters.n: His officials said even more against the Lord God and His servant Hezekiah.
Sennacherib also wrote letters mocking the God of Israel, insisting He could no more save His people than the other gods.

f.g: To insult; to taunt.

chapters.n: They shouted in Hebrew to the people on the walls to frighten and demoralize them so the city would surrender.

f.g: In Hebrew, the people’s language, rather than the diplomatic Aramaic.
To terrify them.

chapters.n: They spoke of Jerusalem’s God as if He were one of the man-made gods of the nations. That was their fatal error.

f.w: the work of the hands of man

chapters.n: So King Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah prayed and cried out to heaven. King and prophet united in prayer.

f.w: the prophet Isaiah the son of Amoz

chapters.n: The Lord sent an angel who destroyed the Assyrian warriors and commanders. Sennacherib went home in disgrace, and later his own sons killed him in his god’s temple.

f.g: 2 Kings 19:35 records 185,000 Assyrians slain in one night.

f.w: they that came forth of his own bowels slew him
f.g: His own sons murdered him (681 BC).

chapters.n: So the Lord saved Hezekiah and Jerusalem from Sennacherib and all others, and gave them rest on every side.

f.g: Or ‘gave them rest all around.’

chapters.n: Many brought offerings to the Lord and gifts to Hezekiah, and he became highly respected among the nations.

f.g: Exalted; held in high honor.

chapters.n: Around this time Hezekiah became deathly ill. He prayed, and the Lord answered and gave him a sign — the shadow moving backward on the sundial — adding fifteen years to his life.
But Hezekiah didn’t respond with proper gratitude; his heart became proud, bringing God’s displeasure on him and Judah. Even the faithful can stumble after great blessings.

f.w: rendered not again according to the benefit
f.g: Did not respond in gratitude for the kindness shown him.

chapters.n: Then Hezekiah and Jerusalem humbled themselves over their pride, so God’s anger didn’t come in his lifetime.
Hezekiah had great wealth and honor and built treasuries for silver, gold, gems, spices, shields, and valuables.

f.g: Desirable, precious objects.

chapters.n: He also built storehouses for grain, wine, and oil, and stalls and pens for livestock.

f.g: Sheepfolds or pens.

chapters.n: He acquired towns and large flocks and herds, for God had given him great wealth.
Hezekiah blocked the upper outlet of the Gihon spring and channeled the water down to the west side of the City of David — the famous tunnel through solid rock, still walkable in Jerusalem today.

f.g: Hezekiah’s Tunnel, about 1,750 feet (533 m) long, carved to bring water to the Pool of Siloam; an ancient Hebrew inscription inside describes its completion.

chapters.n: When Babylonian envoys came to ask about the miracle, God left Hezekiah to himself to test him and reveal what was in his heart. He proudly showed them all his treasures.

f.w: the ambassadors of the princes of Babylon
to try him, that he might know all that was in his heart

chapters.n: Hezekiah’s other acts and his good deeds are recorded in the vision of Isaiah and in the book of the kings.

f.w: the vision of Isaiah the prophet

chapters.n: Hezekiah was buried with great honor in the upper section of the royal tombs, mourned by all Judah. His son Manasseh succeeded him.

f.g: The highest or most honored place among the royal tombs.

chapters.n: Manasseh became king at just twelve and reigned fifty-five years (about 697–642 BC, including a co-regency) — the longest reign of any king of Judah.
He did evil, copying the detestable practices of the nations God had driven out of the land.
Manasseh undid his father’s reforms: he rebuilt the high places, set up Baal altars and Asherah poles, and worshipped the stars.

f.g: The sun, moon, and stars, worshipped especially in Assyrian religion.

chapters.n: He even built pagan altars inside the Lord’s temple — the very place God had chosen for His name forever.

f.w: In Jerusalem shall my name be for ever

chapters.n: He built altars to the stars in both temple courtyards.
He sacrificed his own children in fire in the Valley of Hinnom and practiced fortune-telling, sorcery, witchcraft, and consulting mediums and spiritists — everything the law forbade.

f.g: Practiced soothsaying or reading omens.
A medium who claimed to speak with the dead.

chapters.n: He placed a carved idol in God’s house — the house God had promised to make the dwelling of His name forever.

f.g: Probably an Asherah image.

chapters.n: God had promised never again to uproot Israel from the land — if they would carefully keep His law. The promise was conditional.

f.w: so that they will take heed
f.g: On condition that they obey.

chapters.n: Manasseh led Judah astray until they were worse than the nations God had destroyed. Leaders shape a people for good or ill.

f.g: To go astray.

chapters.n: God spoke to Manasseh and his people through prophets, but they refused to listen.
So God brought Assyrian commanders who captured Manasseh with hooks, bound him in bronze chains, and took him to Babylon (then under Assyrian rule).

f.g: Probably ‘with hooks’ — Assyrians sometimes led captives by hooks through the nose or lip.
Bronze shackles.

chapters.n: In his distress Manasseh sought the Lord and deeply humbled himself before the God of his ancestors. Affliction turned his heart.
He prayed, and God was moved by his plea, heard him, and brought him back to his kingdom. Then Manasseh knew that the Lord is God. No one is beyond the reach of repentance.

f.g: God was moved by his prayer.

f.w: Manasseh knew that the LORD he was God

chapters.n: Back home, he built an outer wall for the City of David, from the Gihon spring to the Fish Gate and around Ophel, and placed commanders in Judah’s fortified cities.
He removed the foreign gods, the idol from the temple, and the altars he had built, throwing them out of the city. True repentance undoes past wrongs.
He restored the Lord’s altar, offered peace and thank offerings, and commanded Judah to serve the God of Israel.
The people still sacrificed at high places, but only to the Lord. Bad habits outlast a king’s change of heart.
Manasseh’s other deeds, his prayer, and the prophets’ words to him are recorded in the book of the kings. (A later work called the “Prayer of Manasseh” imagines his prayer.)

f.g: The text of his prayer isn’t preserved in the Bible; a later apocryphal ‘Prayer of Manasseh’ was composed in his name.

chapters.n: His prayer, God’s response, his sins, and the sites of his idolatry before he humbled himself are recorded among the sayings of the seers.

f.g: Some manuscripts read ‘Hozai,’ the name of a seer.

chapters.n: Manasseh died and was buried at his palace, not in the royal tombs. His son Amon succeeded him.

f.g: 2 Kings 21:18 says in the garden of Uzza at his palace.

chapters.n: Amon became king at twenty-two and reigned only two years.
Amon did evil like his father, worshipping all the idols Manasseh had made.
Unlike his father, Amon never humbled himself before the Lord — he sinned more and more. Manasseh’s late repentance did not pass to his son.
His officials conspired against him and killed him in his palace.
The people of the land executed the conspirators and made his eight-year-old son Josiah king.

f.g: The landowning citizens of Judah, who often acted to protect David’s line.

chapters.n: Josiah became king at eight and reigned thirty-one years (about 640–609 BC). His reign was the last great revival before Judah’s fall.

f.g: His birth and reforms were prophesied about 300 years earlier.

chapters.n: He did right and followed David’s ways, turning neither right nor left — steady, unwavering obedience.

f.w: declined neither to the right hand, nor to the left

chapters.n: At sixteen (his eighth year), while still young, he began to seek David’s God. At twenty he began purging Judah and Jerusalem of high places, Asherah poles, and idols. Personal conversion came first, then public reform.
In his presence they tore down Baal altars and incense altars, crushed the idols to dust, and scattered the dust on the graves of those who had worshipped them.

f.g: Scattered; strewed.
Incense altars (Hebrew hammanim).

chapters.n: He burned the bones of pagan priests on their own altars, defiling those altars forever — exactly as a prophet had foretold three centuries earlier. Thus he cleansed Judah and Jerusalem.

f.w: he burnt the bones of the priests upon their altars

chapters.n: He extended his reform north into the old territories of Manasseh, Ephraim, Simeon, and Naphtali — lands of the former northern kingdom, now weakened Assyrian provinces.

f.g: The Hebrew is uncertain; often read ‘in their ruins round about.’

chapters.n: After destroying altars, poles, and idols throughout the land of Israel, he returned to Jerusalem.

f.w: beaten the graven images into powder

chapters.n: In his eighteenth year (about 622 BC), having cleansed land and temple, he sent officials to repair the Lord’s house.

f.g: A royal secretary whose family later protected the prophet Jeremiah.
The royal herald or chronicler.

chapters.n: They delivered to Hilkiah the high priest the money collected by Levite doorkeepers from Manasseh, Ephraim, the rest of Israel, Judah, and Benjamin — a nationwide offering.
The money was given to supervisors who paid the workers repairing the temple.

f.g: Repair; restore.

chapters.n: Carpenters and builders used it to buy cut stone and timber for beams and to rebuild what earlier kings had let decay.

f.g: Beams or joists.
Craftsmen.

chapters.n: The workers labored faithfully under Levite overseers from Merari and Kohath, including skilled musicians.

f.g: Honestly — no accounting was required of them.

chapters.n: Levites also supervised the laborers and served as scribes, officials, and gatekeepers.

f.g: Gatekeepers.

chapters.n: While taking out the money, Hilkiah found the book of the Lord’s law given through Moses — likely a scroll of Deuteronomy, lost or hidden during Manasseh’s long apostasy.

f.w: a book of the law of the LORD given by Moses
f.g: Many scholars identify it with Deuteronomy or a core of it, based on Josiah’s reforms.

chapters.n: Hilkiah told Shaphan, “I found the book of the law in the temple,” and gave it to him. Lost scripture recovered is a theme Latter-day Saints know well.

f.w: I have found the book of the law

chapters.n: Shaphan brought the book to the king and first reported that the work was going as ordered.
He reported that the money had been given to the overseers and workers.
Then, almost as an afterthought, Shaphan mentioned the book and read it aloud to the king.
Hearing God’s law, Josiah tore his clothes in grief — realizing how far Judah had strayed. Scripture pricked his heart.

f.g: Tearing garments was a sign of grief and repentance.

chapters.n: Josiah sent five trusted officials, including Hilkiah and Shaphan’s son Ahikam, on an urgent mission.
He told them: inquire of the Lord for me and for those left in Israel and Judah about this book, for His great anger is upon us because our fathers didn’t obey it.

f.w: them that are left in Israel
f.g: The remnant of the northern tribes after the Assyrian exile.

chapters.n: They went to the prophetess Huldah, who lived in Jerusalem’s newer quarter. Her husband was keeper of the royal or priestly wardrobe. God spoke through a faithful woman prophet.

f.g: Hebrew mishneh — the ‘second quarter,’ a newer district of Jerusalem.

chapters.n: Huldah answered with authority: “Thus saith the LORD God of Israel, tell the man who sent you…”
God will bring disaster on Jerusalem and its people — all the curses written in the book read to the king.

f.w: all the curses that are written in the book

chapters.n: Because they abandoned Him and worshipped other gods, His wrath would pour out and not be quenched. The judgment was now certain.
But to the king who sent you to ask the Lord, say this concerning the words he has heard:
Because your heart was tender and you humbled yourself, tore your clothes, and wept before Me when you heard My words, I have heard you. A tender heart moves God.
You will die in peace and not see the disaster. The messengers reported back to the king. (Josiah died in battle, but before Jerusalem’s destruction.)

f.w: gathered to thy grave in peace
f.g: Josiah would not live to see Jerusalem’s fall, though he died in battle.

chapters.n: Rather than giving up, the king called together all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem. Even knowing judgment was coming, he chose to lead his people to God.
Josiah went to the temple with everyone — priests, Levites, and people great and small — and read aloud the whole book of the covenant. The king himself became a teacher of scripture.
Standing in the king’s place, he made a covenant before the Lord to follow Him and keep His commandments with all his heart and soul.

f.g: Probably by the royal pillar.

chapters.n: He had everyone in Jerusalem and Benjamin commit to it, and they lived by God’s covenant.

f.g: To pledge themselves to it.

chapters.n: Josiah removed every abomination from Israel’s lands and led everyone to serve the Lord. As long as he lived, they did not turn away. But the reform seems to have depended heavily on him.
Josiah held a Passover in Jerusalem on the fourteenth day of the first month — the proper time, unlike Hezekiah’s delayed one.

f.w: the fourteenth day of the first month

chapters.n: He assigned the priests to their duties and encouraged them in their temple service.

f.g: Strengthened them.

chapters.n: He told the Levites, who taught Israel, to put the holy ark in Solomon’s temple — no more carrying it on their shoulders — and serve God and His people. This is the last mention of the ark in the Old Testament historical books.

f.w: Put the holy ark in the house
f.g: The ark may have been removed during Manasseh’s reign; it vanishes from history after this.

f.w: the Levites that taught all Israel

chapters.n: Prepare by your family divisions according to the written instructions of David and Solomon.
Stand in the holy place in groups to serve each family of the people.
Slaughter the Passover lambs, purify yourselves, and prepare for your fellow Israelites to obey the Lord’s word through Moses.
Josiah personally donated 30,000 lambs and goats and 3,000 cattle for the people’s Passover — from his own possessions.

f.g: The king’s own property.

chapters.n: His officials gave willingly too. The temple leaders Hilkiah, Zechariah, and Jehiel gave the priests 2,600 small animals and 300 cattle.

f.g: Sheep and goats.

chapters.n: Levite leaders gave 5,000 small animals and 500 cattle for the Levites’ Passover offerings.
With everything ready, priests and Levites took their places according to the king’s command.
They slaughtered the Passover lambs; the priests sprinkled the blood and the Levites skinned the animals.

f.g: Skinned.

chapters.n: They set aside the burnt-offering portions to distribute by family groups, as Moses’ law prescribed, and did the same with the cattle.
They roasted the Passover lambs as the law required and boiled the other holy offerings in pots, quickly serving everyone.

f.g: Boiled.

chapters.n: Since the priests were busy with offerings until night, the Levites prepared the meal for themselves and the priests.
The singers and gatekeepers stayed at their posts because their fellow Levites prepared their portions. Everyone served in his place.
All the Lord’s service was completed that day, as King Josiah commanded.
Israel kept the Passover and the seven-day Feast of Unleavened Bread.
No Passover like this had been kept since Samuel’s day — not even under any king. Its faithfulness to the law, its scale, and its inclusion of all Israel set it apart.

f.w: from the days of Samuel the prophet

chapters.n: This Passover took place in Josiah’s eighteenth year — the same year the book of the law was found.
Years later (609 BC), Pharaoh Necho marched north to fight at Carchemish on the Euphrates, helping Assyria against Babylon. Josiah went out to stop him.

f.g: Pharaoh Necho II (ruled about 610–595 BC).
A key city on the upper Euphrates, where Babylon decisively defeated Egypt in 605 BC.

chapters.n: Necho sent a message: “I’m not here to fight you but another kingdom. God told me to hurry. Stop opposing God, who is with me, or He will destroy you.”

f.w: forbear thee from meddling with God
f.g: Stop interfering with what God is doing.

chapters.n: Josiah refused to turn back, disguised himself for battle (as Ahab once did), ignored God’s words through Necho, and fought in the valley of Megiddo. Even a righteous man can misjudge where God’s voice is coming from.

f.g: A famous battlefield; later associated with ‘Armageddon.’

chapters.n: Archers shot Josiah, and he told his servants, “Take me away — I’m badly wounded.”

f.g: Severely wounded.

chapters.n: They moved him to his second chariot and brought him to Jerusalem, where he died and was buried in his ancestors’ tombs. All Judah and Jerusalem mourned him.
Jeremiah composed laments for Josiah, and singers commemorated him for generations. His death became a symbol of national mourning.

f.g: A collection of laments, not necessarily the biblical book of Lamentations.

chapters.n: Josiah’s other deeds and his loyal devotion, in keeping with God’s law…

f.g: His acts of covenant faithfulness (Hebrew ḥasadim).

chapters.n: …from beginning to end, are written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah.
After Josiah’s death, the people of the land crowned his son Jehoahaz king in Jerusalem.

f.g: Also called Shallum.

chapters.n: Jehoahaz was twenty-three and reigned only three months (609 BC).
Pharaoh Necho deposed him and imposed a tribute of 100 talents of silver and a talent of gold on Judah. Judah was now an Egyptian vassal.

f.g: Imposed a fine or tribute on the land.

chapters.n: Necho made Jehoahaz’s brother Eliakim king, renamed him Jehoiakim — a sign of Egypt’s control — and took Jehoahaz to Egypt, where he died.

f.g: Renaming showed the overlord’s authority over him.

chapters.n: Jehoiakim became king at twenty-five, reigned eleven years (609–598 BC), and did evil. He burned Jeremiah’s scroll and persecuted prophets.
Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon, now the dominant power, came against him and bound him in bronze chains to take him to Babylon.

f.g: Ruled about 605–562 BC; defeated Egypt at Carchemish in 605.

chapters.n: Nebuchadnezzar took some temple vessels and put them in his temple in Babylon. These vessels would later be returned under Cyrus.

f.w: the vessels of the house of the LORD

chapters.n: Jehoiakim’s detestable deeds are recorded in the book of the kings. His son Jehoiachin succeeded him.

f.w: that which was found in him
f.g: The evil discovered in him.

chapters.n: Jehoiachin reigned three months and ten days (598–597 BC) and did evil. The text says eight years old, but 2 Kings says eighteen, which fits better.

f.g: 2 Kings 24:8 and some ancient versions read eighteen.
Also called Jeconiah or Coniah.

chapters.n: At the turn of the year, Nebuchadnezzar took Jehoiachin to Babylon with the finest temple vessels, and made Zedekiah — Jehoiachin’s uncle — king. Ezekiel and Daniel were among early exiles.

f.g: Literally his relative — Zedekiah was Josiah’s son, Jehoiachin’s uncle.

chapters.n: Zedekiah became king at twenty-one and reigned eleven years (597–586 BC). In his first year, Lehi began to prophesy in Jerusalem and soon fled with his family, beginning the Book of Mormon story.
Zedekiah did evil and refused to humble himself before Jeremiah, who spoke for the Lord. Lehi was one of the “many prophets” of this time.

f.w: humbled not himself before Jeremiah the prophet

chapters.n: He also broke his sworn oath of loyalty to Nebuchadnezzar, made in God’s name. Stubbornly he hardened his heart against returning to the Lord.

f.w: who had made him swear by God

f.g: Became stubborn and unbending.

chapters.n: The leading priests and people also became deeply unfaithful, copying the nations’ abominations and defiling the temple God had made holy. Ezekiel saw such idolatry in a vision.

f.w: polluted the house of the LORD

chapters.n: Yet God, out of compassion for His people and His house, kept sending messengers again and again — “rising up betimes” means early and persistently.

f.g: Getting up early — persistently and earnestly.

chapters.n: But they mocked God’s messengers, despised His words, and abused His prophets until His anger rose and there was no remedy. Lehi too was mocked and threatened.

f.w: they mocked the messengers of God

f.g: Until there was no healing left.

chapters.n: So God brought the Babylonian (Chaldean) king, who killed young men even in the sanctuary and showed no mercy to young or old (586 BC).

f.g: The Chaldeans were the ruling dynasty of Babylon.

chapters.n: He carried all the temple vessels and the treasures of the temple, king, and officials to Babylon.
They burned God’s house, broke down Jerusalem’s walls, burned its palaces, and destroyed everything valuable. Solomon’s temple was gone, just as God had warned.

f.w: they burnt the house of God

chapters.n: Survivors were taken to Babylon as servants of the king and his sons until Persia rose to power (539 BC).

f.w: until the reign of the kingdom of Persia

chapters.n: This fulfilled Jeremiah’s prophecy: the land would rest seventy years, making up for the Sabbath years Israel had neglected. God’s law of rest for the land was finally kept by force.

f.w: until the land had enjoyed her sabbaths

chapters.n: But the story ends in hope: in Cyrus of Persia’s first year (538 BC), to fulfill Jeremiah’s word, God moved Cyrus to issue a written decree throughout his empire. Isaiah had even named Cyrus long before.

f.g: Founder of the Persian Empire; conquered Babylon in 539 BC.

chapters.n: Cyrus declared that the God of heaven gave him all kingdoms and charged him to build a house in Jerusalem: whoever belongs to His people may go up — the Lord be with them. The Hebrew Bible ends on this word of return: “let him go up.”

f.g: In the Hebrew Bible’s order, Chronicles is the last book, so the scriptures end with this invitation to return.
